baselines.name: OGRL NIST SP 800-171 Rev 3 Core Baseline

controls.name: Account Provisioning and Lifecycle Governance
controls.summary: Require documented approval before provisioning user or service accounts and disable accounts promptly upon departure.
controls.statement: Approve every user and service account request through {{ approver_role }} prior to provisioning, and revoke or disable accounts within {{ deprovision_sla }} of personnel termination or role change.
controls.objective: Ensure only authorized personnel and services hold active accounts on in-scope systems.
controls.guidance: Integrate the identity provider with HR lifecycle events so terminations automatically trigger session revocation and account suspension within the defined SLA.

tests.name: Verify Account Provisioning Approvals and Termination Revocation
tests.description: Confirm newly provisioned accounts have linked approval tickets and all terminated personnel accounts were disabled within the configured deprovisioning SLA.

mappings.summary: Approved identity provisioning and timely offboarding satisfy ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.16.
Approval before provisioning and prompt revocation limit access to authorized users and service accounts; device authorization is out of scope.
Revokes access within a defined SLA on termination or role change; return of physical credentials and other transfer protections are not covered.
Account provisioning approval and termination revocation contribute to SP 800-171 03.01.01 account management.
Pre-provisioning account approval directly satisfies NIST AC-2(e).
Timely termination deprovisioning satisfies NIST AC-2(h.2) notification and suspension timing.
Documented provisioning approval and prompt deprovisioning satisfy SOC 2 CC6.2.
Revoking or modifying access on termination and role change addresses the removal and modification aspects of CC6.3.

controls.name: Periodic User Access Review
controls.summary: Review active user accounts and privileged group memberships on a defined cadence and revoke unapproved access.
controls.statement: Review all active user accounts, privileged roles, and service accounts {{ review_cadence }} and remediate unauthorized or unneeded entitlements within {{ remediation_window }}.
controls.objective: Detect and remove privilege creep, orphaned accounts, and stale entitlements before misuse.
controls.guidance: Generate account rosters directly from authoritative identity providers and production systems, require reviewer sign-off from managers or system owners, and retain ticketed removal evidence.

tests.name: Verify Quarterly Access Review Completion
tests.description: Examine completed quarterly user access review records to confirm reviewer sign-off and timely removal of revoked entitlements.

mappings.summary: Periodic user access reviews and revocation satisfy ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.18.
Periodic user access reviews contribute to SP 800-171 03.01.01 account compliance reviews.
Periodic user access review directly satisfies NIST AC-2(j) account compliance reviews.
Periodic review confirms registered users remain authorized, supporting the credential lifecycle in CC6.2.
Quarterly access reviews and timely entitlement removal satisfy SOC 2 CC6.3.

controls.name: Least Privilege and Role-Based Access Enforcement
controls.summary: Enforce least-privilege role-based access control so users and services receive only permissions required for their job function.
controls.statement: Restrict logical access to systems, administrative interfaces, and sensitive data using role-based access control scoped to least privilege, requiring {{ privileged_elevation }} for administrative actions.
controls.objective: Limit blast radius by preventing unauthorized read, write, or administrative operations.
controls.guidance: Avoid standing administrative privileges on production environments; use scoped IAM roles, just-in-time elevation, and separation between developer and production-deployment permissions.

tests.name: Verify Least-Privilege Role Assignments
tests.description: Check IAM role bindings and administrative group memberships to verify no unauthorized wildcard permissions or standing administrative privileges exist.

mappings.summary: Least-privilege RBAC policies directly satisfy ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.15.
Role-based access scoped to least privilege defines and limits the functions each user may execute.
Enforces least-privilege access and elevation for administrative actions; identification of privileged accounts and security functions is handled elsewhere.
Least-privilege role enforcement directly satisfies SP 800-171 03.01.05.
Role-based access control enforces approved logical access authorizations per AC-3.
Least-privilege role scoping and just-in-time elevation satisfy NIST AC-6.
Least-privilege RBAC and access enforcement satisfy SOC 2 CC6.1 logical access security.
Role-based least privilege governs how access is granted and modified under CC6.3.

controls.name: Network Boundary and Logical Access Restriction
controls.summary: Segment network boundaries with default-deny ingress controls and restrict administrative ports from the public internet.
controls.statement: Enforce default-deny network ingress policies at system boundaries, allowing only explicitly documented service ports and restricting administrative access to {{ admin_access_path }}.
controls.objective: Prevent unauthorized network traffic and direct internet exposure of internal or administrative services.
controls.guidance: Manage security groups, firewall rules, and private network peering via infrastructure-as-code with automated drift detection.

admin_access_path.label: Authorized administrative network path
admin_access_path.value: authenticated VPN or zero-trust bastion endpoints

tests.name: Verify Default-Deny Network Ingress Policies
tests.description: Inspect cloud security groups and firewall rules to confirm administrative ports (SSH, RDP, database ports) are not exposed to 0.0.0.0/0.

mappings.summary: Controls ingress at system boundaries and restricts administrative paths; boundary definition, monitoring, and egress and internal boundary controls are not covered.
Default-deny boundaries restrict exposure; placing public components in separate subnetworks is not required.
Denies inbound traffic by default and permits documented exceptions; outbound default-deny is not covered.
Default-deny network restrictions form part of the logical access security architecture in CC6.1.
Default-deny network boundaries and restricted admin paths satisfy SOC 2 CC6.6.

controls.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Enforcement
controls.summary: Require phishing-resistant or hardware-backed multi-factor authentication for all interactive user and privileged logins.
controls.statement: Enforce {{ mfa_standard }} multi-factor authentication on all interactive workforce, remote, and privileged accounts across identity providers and in-scope systems.
controls.objective: Prevent account compromise from stolen, reused, or phished single-factor credentials.
controls.guidance: Prefer FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys or platform authenticators for privileged accounts, and block legacy single-factor protocols.

tests.name: Verify MFA Enforcement on All Active Accounts
tests.description: Query the identity provider and cloud IAM directories to confirm MFA is enrolled and enforced for 100% of active interactive accounts.

mappings.summary: Phishing-resistant MFA enforcement satisfies ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.5 secure authentication.
MFA authenticates interactive users; authentication of processes and devices is not covered.
Enforces MFA on all interactive workforce, remote, and privileged accounts, covering local and network access.
MFA enforcement across interactive and privileged logins satisfies SP 800-171 03.05.03.
Universal MFA enforcement satisfies and strengthens organizational user authentication under IA-2.
Universal MFA strengthens authentication required by SOC 2 CC6.1.

controls.name: Secret and Authenticator Lifecycle Management
controls.summary: Store secrets in managed vaults, prohibit hardcoded credentials, and rotate keys on a defined cadence or upon compromise.
controls.statement: Manage passwords, API keys, and cryptographic credentials in an approved secrets vault, rotate non-ephemeral credentials at least every {{ rotation_period }}, and revoke immediately upon {{ revocation_triggers }}.
controls.objective: Protect authenticators from unauthorized disclosure and limit exposure windows if leaked.
controls.guidance: Prefer short-lived workload identities (OIDC/IAM roles) over static API keys, run secret scanning on source repositories, and replace default credentials prior to deployment.

revocation_triggers.label: Immediate revocation events
revocation_triggers.value: suspected exposure, personnel departure, or system decommission

tests.name: Verify Secret Vaulting and Credential Rotation Age
tests.description: Confirm static API keys and service credentials do not exceed the configured rotation age and repository secret scanning reports zero unresolved leaks.

mappings.summary: Vaulted secret storage and rotation governance satisfy ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.17.
Manages password lifecycle and rotation; immediate change of temporary passwords at first logon is not covered.
Scheduled credential rotation and event-driven revocation directly satisfy NIST IA-5(f).
Protecting secrets and credentials is part of the logical access safeguards in CC6.1.

controls.name: Privileged Access Management
controls.summary: Limit administrative access to an approved roster, separate it from everyday accounts, alert on changes, and reconcile it regularly.
controls.statement: Maintain an approved roster of individuals authorized to hold administrative access to {{ privileged_scope }}, limited to {{ privileged_roles }}; require those individuals to use dedicated privileged accounts or elevated roles that are not used for email, browsing, or other routine work; alert {{ privileged_alert_recipient }} on every grant of a privileged role and every change to a privileged role definition; and reconcile actual privileged assignments against the roster {{ privileged_review_frequency }}, removing any that are not approved.
controls.objective: Keep the set of people who can alter security configurations, production systems, or audit data small, known, and monitored.
controls.guidance: Define privileged roles in the identity provider and cloud IAM and treat cloud root, organization admin, IdP super-admin, database superuser, and security tooling admin as in scope. Use separate admin identities or just-in-time role elevation (see OGRL-AC-03) instead of permanently privileged daily accounts. Stream IAM and IdP role-change events to the SIEM for alerting, and export privileged group membership for the reconciliation. Break-glass accounts belong on the roster with sealed credentials and alerting on use.

privileged_roles.label: Personnel eligible for privileged access
privileged_roles.value: named members of the infrastructure and security teams

privileged_scope.label: Systems and functions treated as privileged
privileged_scope.value: cloud provider organizations, identity provider administration, production databases, and security tooling

mappings.summary: Authorizes who may hold privileged access; it does not address remote execution of privileged commands or remote access to security-relevant information specifically.
The privileged roster identifies privileged accounts and limits them to approved people; general least privilege is in OGRL-AC-03, and alerting goes beyond 3.1.5.
Requires dedicated privileged accounts or roles that are not used for email, browsing, or other routine work.
Limits privileged functions to an approved roster; logging of privileged function execution is not covered.
Role-based privileged accounts, alerting on privileged assignments and role changes, and removal of unapproved privileges cover AC-2(7).
The approved roster explicitly authorizes which individuals may access security functions and security-relevant systems.
Dedicated privileged accounts or elevated roles are not used for routine, non-security work.
Privileged accounts are restricted to the defined set of eligible personnel.
Periodic reconciliation of privileged assignments validates need and removes unapproved privileges; non-privileged access review is in OGRL-AC-02.
Restricting and monitoring administrative access contributes to logical access protection under CC6.1.
Limiting privileged roles to approved individuals applies least privilege to the most sensitive access under CC6.3.

controls.name: Separation of Duties
controls.summary: Document conflicting duties and configure access so no single person can complete a conflicting pair alone.
controls.statement: Document the duties that must be separated, including at minimum {{ separated_duties }}, configure system access so that no single individual can perform both duties in a conflicting pair without independent approval, and record any approved exception together with its compensating control.
controls.objective: Prevent a single individual from introducing and concealing unauthorized or erroneous changes.
controls.guidance: Enforce separation technically where possible: branch protection requiring a reviewer other than the author, access-request workflows that block self-approval, and audit log storage that system administrators cannot modify. Small teams that cannot fully separate duties should document compensating detective controls such as after-the-fact review of administrator activity.

separated_duties.label: Duties that must be separated
separated_duties.value: authoring and approving production code changes, requesting and approving access grants, and administering systems and reviewing their audit logs

mappings.summary: Documents conflicting duties and assigns them, and the access that enables them, to separate individuals.
Documenting separated duties and configuring access authorizations to enforce them satisfies both parts of AC-5.
Segregating incompatible duties is a control activity that mitigates risk under CC5.1.
Separation of duties is a consideration when authorizing and modifying role-based access under CC6.3.

controls.name: Inactive and Temporary Account Disablement
controls.summary: Automatically disable dormant, expired, orphaned, and temporary accounts.
controls.statement: Automatically disable user accounts that have been inactive for {{ inactivity_period }}; disable accounts that have expired, are no longer associated with an active individual, or violate policy within {{ disable_window }} of detection; and configure temporary and emergency accounts to be {{ temporary_account_action }} automatically after {{ temporary_account_lifetime }}.
controls.objective: Eliminate dormant and leftover accounts that could be used for unauthorized access.
controls.guidance: Use identity provider inactivity policies or a scheduled job that compares last-login data from the IdP and directly-managed systems against the threshold. Set expiration dates on contractor, vendor-support, and break-glass accounts at creation. Service accounts are excluded from the inactivity rule but must have an owner and appear in access reviews (OGRL-AC-02).

disable_window.label: Time to disable expired, orphaned, or non-compliant accounts

temporary_account_lifetime.label: Maximum temporary or emergency account lifetime
temporary_account_lifetime.value: the approved expiration date, not to exceed 30 days

mappings.summary: Automatically disables accounts after a defined inactivity period.
Temporary and emergency accounts are automatically disabled or removed after a defined period.
Disabling expired, orphaned, non-compliant, and inactive accounts within a defined window covers all of AC-2(3).
Removing dormant and temporary accounts supports deregistration of users who no longer need access under CC6.2.

controls.name: Session Lock and Termination
controls.summary: Lock idle workstations and terminate idle or long-lived sessions to in-scope systems.
controls.statement: Configure workforce endpoints to lock the screen after {{ device_lock_timeout }} of inactivity, requiring re-authentication to unlock, and configure in-scope applications, administrative consoles, and remote access sessions to terminate after {{ session_termination_conditions }}.
controls.objective: Prevent unattended or hijacked sessions from being used to access systems and data.
controls.guidance: Enforce screen lock through MDM configuration profiles and session lifetimes through identity provider and cloud console session policies. Apply shorter timeouts to production and administrative access than to collaboration tools. Evidence is typically the MDM profile, IdP session policy, and cloud console session settings.

session_termination_conditions.label: Session termination conditions
session_termination_conditions.value: 30 minutes of inactivity or 12 hours of total session duration

mappings.summary: Locks idle endpoints with re-authentication; pattern-hiding displays are not explicitly required.
Automatically terminates application, console, and remote sessions after defined inactivity or duration conditions.
Terminates application and remote sessions after inactivity; termination of the underlying network connections is not stated.
Inactivity-based screen lock that persists until re-authentication satisfies AC-11.
Sessions to in-scope systems are automatically terminated under defined conditions.
Session lock and termination is one logical access safeguard within CC6.1.

controls.name: Remote Access Security
controls.summary: Document and authorize each remote access method and route production remote access through an approved, authenticated gateway.
controls.statement: Document each permitted remote access method to in-scope systems with its usage restrictions and configuration requirements, authorize each method before it is enabled, and require all remote access to production environments to pass through {{ remote_access_gateway }} that enforces single sign-on with multi-factor authentication, encrypted transport, and session logging; review the permitted methods {{ remote_access_review_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Ensure remote connections to production are made only through known, approved, and monitored paths.
controls.guidance: For cloud SaaS, remote access usually means administrative paths into production: cloud consoles and CLIs, SSH or database sessions via a bastion or identity-aware proxy, and Kubernetes API access. Prefer identity-aware proxies or SSM-style session managers over static SSH keys and public bastions. Network-level exposure restrictions are covered by OGRL-AC-04.

remote_access_gateway.label: Approved remote access gateway
remote_access_gateway.value: an approved identity-aware proxy, session manager, or VPN

mappings.summary: Documents and authorizes remote access methods and logs gateway sessions; active monitoring is not stated and the gateway requirement covers production only.
Requires encrypted transport for remote access through the gateway; encryption is not explicitly required for every remote method outside production.
Routes production remote access through a managed gateway; other in-scope remote access is not explicitly routed.
Authorizes remote access methods; specific privileged commands and security-relevant information allowed remotely are not identified or authorized.
Documented restrictions and configuration requirements per remote access type, with authorization before enablement, satisfy AC-17.
Authenticated, logged remote access gateways contribute to logical access security under CC6.1.
Controlling remote access paths into production protects against threats from outside system boundaries under CC6.6.

controls.name: Information Flow Enforcement and Tenant Data Segregation
controls.summary: Scope every data path to the requesting customer's tenant and test isolation on each release.
controls.statement: Enforce tenant isolation in every data path of the service so that each request, query, background job, and export is constrained to the authenticated customer's tenant at {{ isolation_enforcement_layer }}, and run automated cross-tenant access tests {{ isolation_test_trigger }}.
controls.objective: Prevent one customer's data from flowing to, or being accessed by, another customer.
controls.guidance: Enforce tenancy in a shared layer rather than in each handler: row-level security, tenant-scoped repository or ORM helpers, per-tenant encryption keys, or per-tenant databases. Derive the tenant from the authenticated session, never from client-supplied parameters alone. Include cross-tenant negative tests in CI and in periodic penetration tests.

isolation_enforcement_layer.label: Layer where tenant isolation is enforced
isolation_enforcement_layer.value: the data access layer through row-level security or mandatory tenant-scoped queries

mappings.summary: Tenant isolation enforces one kind of information flow restriction; CUI flow policies, designated sources and destinations, and flow authorizations are not covered.
Prevents cross-tenant data transfer through shared data stores and services; residual data in other shared resources is not covered.
Tenant isolation enforces one information flow policy within the system; network and inter-system flow controls are outside this control.
Preventing cross-tenant exposure helps protect customers' confidential information under C1.1.
Segregating customer data at the application layer is a logical access protection within CC6.1.

controls.name: Unique Identification and Centralized SSO
controls.summary: Give every workforce member one unique identity in a central identity provider and use it to sign in to in-scope systems.
controls.statement: Assign each workforce member a unique identifier in {{ identity_provider }}, authenticate access to in-scope systems through single sign-on from that provider wherever the system supports it, prohibit shared or generic user identifiers other than inventoried service and break-glass accounts, and do not reassign a retired identifier for {{ identifier_reuse_period }}.
controls.objective: Make every action on in-scope systems attributable to one individual and manageable from one place.
controls.guidance: Connect SaaS and cloud consoles to the IdP via SAML or OIDC and provision via SCIM where available. Maintain an inventory of in-scope systems that cannot use SSO, with compensating local account management. Do not recycle email addresses or usernames of departed personnel. MFA requirements are in OGRL-AC-05; account approval is in OGRL-AC-01.

identifier_reuse_period.label: Minimum period before an identifier may be reused

identity_provider.label: Central workforce identity provider
identity_provider.value: the organization's designated workforce identity provider

mappings.summary: Unique identities and SSO identify users and gate their access; devices are not addressed, and identifier reuse rules go beyond 3.1.1.
Unique identities make actions attributable; defining audit record content and ensuring records include it is not covered.
Identifies each user and limits shared identifiers to inventoried service accounts; device identification is not covered.
SSO authenticates users before access to in-scope systems; process and device authentication is not covered.
Prohibits reassigning a retired identifier for a defined period.
Unique workforce identities authenticated through central SSO provide unique identification and authentication of organizational users.
Each identifier is selected to identify one specific individual.
Each unique identifier is assigned to the intended individual in the central identity provider.
Retired identifiers are not reused for a defined period.
Unique identities and centralized authentication are foundational logical access measures under CC6.1.
Central identity registration supports the user registration aspect of CC6.2; authorization and removal are other controls.

controls.name: Authenticator Strength and Lockout
controls.summary: Enforce modern password requirements and lock out repeated failed sign-in attempts on every system that accepts passwords.
controls.statement: Configure every in-scope system that accepts passwords, including the identity provider and customer-facing sign-in, to enforce {{ password_composition_rules }}, permit passphrases of at least 64 characters, reject passwords found on a list of breached or commonly used values that is updated {{ blocklist_update_frequency }}, transmit passwords only over encrypted channels, store them only with a salted adaptive key derivation function, require a new password after account recovery, and lock the account or impose increasing delays after {{ max_failed_attempts }} consecutive failed attempts within {{ failed_attempt_window }}.
controls.objective: Resist credential guessing, stuffing, and offline cracking attacks against password-based authentication.
controls.guidance: Follow NIST SP 800-63B: favor length and breached-password screening over composition rules and periodic forced rotation. Use a breached-password service (for example k-anonymity range queries) at creation and change. Use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2id for storage. Apply lockout or rate limiting per account and per source to blunt credential stuffing without enabling easy denial of service.

password_composition_rules.label: Password composition rules
password_composition_rules.value: a minimum length of 12 characters without arbitrary character-class requirements

mappings.summary: Locks accounts or adds delays after a defined number of failed sign-in attempts, alongside other password requirements.
Transmits passwords only over encrypted channels and stores them only with a salted adaptive key derivation function.
Enforces defined password rules at creation; a minimum change of characters between passwords is not required.
Enforces password rules but does not itself prohibit reuse; coverage depends on password composition rules that include a password history.
Requires a new password after account recovery; forced change of other temporary or initial passwords is not stated.
A limit on consecutive failed attempts within a window with automatic lockout or delay satisfies AC-7.
Covers blocklist maintenance and checking, protected transmission and storage, reset on recovery, long passphrases, and composition rules; automated strength-assistance tooling is not required.
Password strength and lockout settings are authentication safeguards within CC6.1.

controls.name: Customer Authentication
controls.summary: Authenticate every customer user uniquely and offer strong authentication options in the product.
controls.statement: Require every customer user of the service to authenticate with an individual account, offer {{ customer_mfa_options }} to all customer users and SAML or OIDC single sign-on to {{ sso_eligible_customers }}, verify the requester through a previously registered channel before completing account recovery, and invalidate active sessions on logout, password change, and account recovery.
controls.objective: Ensure only the intended customer users can access customer accounts and data in the service.
controls.guidance: Use a mature authentication library or customer identity platform rather than custom code. Allow customer administrators to enforce MFA or SSO for their organization. Issue short-lived, server-revocable session tokens. API keys issued to customers should be scoped, revocable, and attributable to a customer account.

customer_mfa_options.label: MFA options offered to customers
customer_mfa_options.value: TOTP authenticator apps and WebAuthn passkeys

mappings.summary: Individual customer accounts uniquely identify and authenticate non-organizational users, with added MFA, SSO, and recovery safeguards.
Customer authentication safeguards protect the service's logical access boundary under CC6.1.

controls.name: System Use Notification Banners
controls.summary: Display an approved privacy and security notice consistent with applicable CUI rules before users can sign in to in-scope systems.
controls.statement: Identify the privacy and security notice requirements that apply to each CUI category and contract handled by in-scope systems and record which notice applies to which category; display an approved system use notification containing {{ banner_content }} at every interactive sign-in to in-scope endpoints, identity provider, remote access gateways, and administrative consoles, keeping it on screen until the user explicitly acknowledges it before access is granted; and review the notice text {{ banner_review_frequency }} and whenever applicable CUI rules or contract clauses change.
controls.objective: Ensure every user is informed of monitoring, permitted use, and CUI handling obligations before accessing systems that hold CUI.
controls.guidance: Have counsel or the contracts lead approve one standard banner and reuse it everywhere. Deploy it through MDM (Windows legal notice policy, macOS login window text), the identity provider sign-in page or custom terms of use, VPN or ZTNA client prompts, SSH pre-authentication banners on servers and network devices, and cloud console sign-in where the provider supports it. Where a SaaS product cannot display a banner itself, enforce sign-in through the identity provider so the IdP banner is shown first. Check each CUI category in the DoD CUI Registry and any DFARS or agency contract clauses for specific notice or marking wording. Evidence is the approved banner text and screenshots or configuration exports showing it on each access path.

banner_content.label: System use notification content
banner_content.value: statements that the system may contain controlled unclassified information, that use may be monitored, recorded, and audited, that unauthorized use is prohibited and subject to criminal and civil penalties, and that use of the system constitutes consent to monitoring and recording

mappings.summary: Identifies CUI-specific notice requirements by category and displays the resulting notice at sign-in, covering both 3.1.9 objectives.

Displays an approved privacy and security notice before access with monitoring, prohibition, and consent statements; the U.S. Government system statement in AC-8(a)(1) is only included if added to the banner content.
Keeps the notice on screen until the user explicitly acknowledges it before access, as AC-8(b) requires.

controls.name: Wireless Access Authorization and Protection
controls.summary: Inventory and authorize every wireless network that reaches in-scope systems and protect it with strong authentication and encryption.
controls.statement: Maintain an inventory of wireless access points and wireless networks that provide access to in-scope systems, document configuration and connection requirements for each type of wireless access, authorize each access point and network before it is enabled, require authentication of {{ wireless_authenticated_entities }} using {{ wireless_authentication_method }} and encryption using {{ wireless_encryption }} on every such network, keep guest and other untrusted wireless networks separated from in-scope systems, and reconcile the inventory against detected access points {{ wireless_review_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Prevent unauthorized or weakly protected wireless connections from providing a path to systems that store or process CUI.
controls.guidance: Use WPA2-Enterprise or WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X backed by the identity provider or certificate-based device authentication instead of shared pre-shared keys for networks that reach CUI. Put guest Wi-Fi on an isolated network with internet-only egress. Most managed wireless controllers and cloud Wi-Fi dashboards can export the access point inventory and report rogue or neighboring access points for the reconciliation. Cloud-first contractors whose offices have no wireless path to in-scope systems should document that all wireless networks, including home and public Wi-Fi, are treated as untrusted and that access to in-scope systems is only through the approved remote access path (OGRL-AC-11); record this scoping decision in the system security plan.

wireless_authentication_method.label: Wireless authentication method
wireless_authentication_method.value: WPA2-Enterprise or WPA3-Enterprise 802.1X with individual user or device credentials

mappings.summary: Inventories wireless access points and authorizes wireless access before connections are allowed.
Requires both authentication and encryption on wireless networks that reach in-scope systems.
Requires authentication of users and devices and encryption on every wireless network reaching in-scope systems.
Documents configuration and connection requirements for each type of wireless access.
Authorizes each wireless access point and network before it is enabled.

controls.name: External System Connections and Use
controls.summary: Identify, verify, and restrict the external systems and devices that connect to in-scope systems or handle CUI.
controls.statement: Maintain an inventory of external systems that connect to in-scope systems or are used to process, store, or transmit organization-controlled information, including cloud services, partner and customer systems, and personally owned devices; permit each connection or use only after {{ external_system_verification }} and approval by {{ external_system_approver }}; prohibit use of {{ prohibited_external_systems }}; enforce the approved list through technical restrictions on connections and data transfer; and re-verify each listed external system {{ external_system_review_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Ensure CUI and in-scope systems are only reached from, or handled by, external systems whose security has been verified and approved.
controls.guidance: For small DIB contractors the inventory is usually the list of cloud services (email, file sharing, ERP, MSP tooling), partner portals, and any personal devices. For cloud services that store or process CUI, verify FedRAMP Moderate authorization or equivalency as required by DFARS 252.204-7012 and keep the customer responsibility matrix. For MSPs and other connected organizations, retain the contract or connection agreement and their CMMC status. Enforce restrictions with conditional access requiring managed or compliant devices, OAuth app consent restrictions, tenant restrictions, and blocking of unapproved storage and sharing services. Treat personally owned devices as prohibited unless they are enrolled and approved, or limited to access that cannot download CUI (for example, browser-only virtual desktop).

external_system_verification.label: Verification required before an external system is permitted
external_system_verification.value: verifying that the external system implements the organization's required security controls, through FedRAMP authorization or equivalency, CMMC certification, or a documented assessment, or retaining an approved connection or processing agreement with its owner

prohibited_external_systems.label: Prohibited types of external systems
prohibited_external_systems.value: personally owned devices and unapproved cloud services for processing, storing, or transmitting CUI

mappings.summary: Identifies, verifies, and technically limits both connections to and use of external systems.
Allows external system use only after control verification or retention of an approved connection or processing agreement.
Permits access from and processing on external systems only after verifying their controls or retaining an agreement with their owner.
Prohibits defined types of external systems.

controls.name: Publicly Accessible Content Review
controls.summary: Restrict who can publish to public systems, review content before posting, and periodically check public content for CUI.
controls.statement: Limit the ability to post or process information on publicly accessible systems to {{ public_content_publishers }}, train each of them to recognize CUI and other nonpublic information before granting publishing rights, require review and approval by a designated reviewer of all proposed content before it is posted, review content on publicly accessible systems for CUI and other nonpublic information {{ public_content_review_frequency }}, and remove any such information discovered within {{ public_content_removal_window }} and report it as a security incident.
controls.objective: Prevent CUI and other nonpublic information from being published or remaining on public websites, social media, and other public systems.
controls.guidance: Publicly accessible systems include the company website, social media accounts, public code repositories, public cloud storage buckets, job postings, and anyone-with-the-link file shares. Enforce the publisher roster through CMS and social media account permissions and repository visibility settings, and block public sharing links in collaboration tools that hold CUI. Use a lightweight ticket or approval step in the CMS for pre-publication review. Evidence is the publisher roster, training records, approval records for recent posts, and the periodic review log.

public_content_publishers.label: Individuals authorized to publish publicly
public_content_publishers.value: named individuals on an approved publisher roster

public_content_removal_window.label: Time to remove improperly posted information

mappings.summary: Designates publishers, reviews content before and after posting, and removes improperly posted CUI.
Restricts publishing on public systems to a designated roster of individuals.
Trains designated publishers to recognize nonpublic information before granting publishing rights.
Requires review of proposed content for nonpublic information before posting.
Reviews public content for nonpublic information on a defined frequency and removes what is found.

controls.name: Authentication Mechanism Protections
controls.summary: Use replay-resistant authentication for network access to accounts and obscure authenticators as they are entered.
controls.statement: Require network authentication to {{ replay_resistant_account_types }} on in-scope systems to use replay-resistant mechanisms such as {{ replay_resistant_mechanisms }}; disable authentication protocols that send reusable secrets in a form that can be captured and replayed, including {{ prohibited_auth_protocols }}; and configure every authentication interface to obscure passwords, PINs, and one-time codes as they are entered.
controls.objective: Prevent captured or observed authentication data from being reused or read to gain access to accounts.
controls.guidance: Modern identity providers using SAML or OIDC with TLS, FIDO2 or WebAuthn, and time-based one-time codes are replay resistant; Kerberos is replay resistant on-premises. Block legacy authentication (basic authentication for mail protocols, NTLMv1 and LM, Telnet, plain FTP, and HTTP basic auth) through IdP conditional access and Group Policy. Password field masking is the default in operating systems and mainstream applications; verify custom applications and command-line tools do not echo secrets, and allow at most a brief user-initiated reveal. Evidence is the IdP legacy authentication policy, protocol configuration, and screenshots of masked sign-in prompts.

prohibited_auth_protocols.label: Prohibited authentication protocols
prohibited_auth_protocols.value: NTLMv1, LM, Telnet, unencrypted FTP, and basic authentication for mail and web protocols

replay_resistant_mechanisms.label: Approved replay-resistant mechanisms
replay_resistant_mechanisms.value: FIDO2/WebAuthn, TLS-protected SAML or OIDC with signed, time-bound assertions, Kerberos, and time-based or challenge-based one-time codes

mappings.summary: Obscures feedback of authentication information during entry.
Requires replay-resistant mechanisms for network access to privileged and non-privileged accounts and disables replayable protocols.
Requires replay-resistant authentication for network access to the defined account types.
Obscures authenticators as they are entered on every authentication interface.

controls.name: Separation of User and System Management Functionality
controls.summary: Keep administrative interfaces separate from the interfaces ordinary users work in.
controls.statement: Document which interfaces of in-scope systems provide user functionality and which provide system management functionality, and provide system management functionality only through {{ management_interface_separation }} that are not exposed through user-facing interfaces and are reachable only by authorized privileged accounts.
controls.objective: Prevent ordinary users and user-facing interfaces from being used to reach or tamper with system administration functions.
controls.guidance: For SaaS and cloud workloads, host internal admin panels on a separate hostname or application behind the identity provider and a restricted network path rather than as hidden routes in the customer-facing app, and keep cloud control-plane access separate from the data plane. On endpoints, users work as standard users and administrative tools run only under separate privileged accounts or elevation (see OGRL-AC-07). Network devices and hypervisors should expose management interfaces only on a management network. Evidence is an architecture diagram or inventory identifying the management interfaces and the configuration that restricts them.

management_interface_separation.label: Means of separating management functionality
management_interface_separation.value: separate administrative consoles, hostnames, or management network paths

mappings.summary: Identifies user and management functionality and separates them.
Identifies management interfaces and keeps them separate from user-facing interfaces.

controls.name: Remote Access Split-Tunneling Prevention
controls.summary: Prevent remotely connected devices from talking to other networks outside the organization's managed tunnel while connected.
controls.statement: Configure the VPN or zero-trust remote access client on every device that connects remotely to in-scope systems so that, while connected, all traffic is routed through the organization's managed tunnel and access to local and other external networks is blocked, prevent users from changing these settings, and permit split tunneling only when the split tunnel is securely provisioned using {{ split_tunnel_safeguards }} and the exception is documented and approved.
controls.objective: Prevent a remote device from bridging the organization's systems to untrusted networks it is simultaneously connected to.
controls.guidance: In most VPN products this is the full-tunnel setting with local LAN access disabled, pushed through MDM or the VPN head-end so users cannot override it. Cloud-delivered secure access service edge (SASE) or ZTNA clients can satisfy the requirement when they steer all device traffic, including internet-bound traffic, through the provider's inspection and policy enforcement. If the organization has no VPN and CUI is reached only through cloud services over TLS, document in the system security plan how remote devices are prevented from bridging networks and expect assessor scrutiny of the approach. Evidence is the client configuration profile and a test showing local network resources are unreachable while connected.

split_tunnel_safeguards.label: Safeguards required for any approved split tunnel
split_tunnel_safeguards.value: a managed cloud security gateway that receives and inspects all non-tunneled traffic and enforces the organization's network policy

mappings.summary: Forces full tunneling and blocks local network access on remote devices; any approved split tunnel must route remaining traffic through managed inspection.
Prevents split tunneling on remote devices unless the tunnel is securely provisioned with defined safeguards.

controls.name: System Component Inventory
controls.summary: Maintain an accurate, owner-assigned inventory of in-scope system components, generated automatically where possible.
controls.statement: Maintain an inventory of in-scope system components, including cloud accounts, compute, data stores, network entry points, workforce endpoints, and production SaaS services, that records {{ inventory_attributes }} for each component and assigns each component to exactly one system and environment. Populate the inventory from provider APIs and device management where available, and reconcile it against those sources {{ inventory_review_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Every component in scope is known, owned, and accounted for once, so that it can be secured, monitored, and assessed.
controls.guidance: Use cloud provider resource inventories, infrastructure-as-code state, MDM enrollment, and the SaaS management or SSO catalog as sources. Required tags (owner, environment, data classification) enforced by policy keep the inventory accurate. Reconciliation means investigating untagged or unknown resources and unenrolled devices. Evidence: an inventory export and reconciliation records.

inventory_attributes.label: Inventory attributes
inventory_attributes.value: unique identifier, type, owner, environment, location or region, and data classification

mappings.summary: Establishes and regularly reconciles a system component inventory; baseline configurations and inventory of software, firmware, and documentation are not addressed.
An accurate, non-duplicated inventory with defined attributes, reconciled on a fixed cadence, covers both parts of the requirement.
The inventory identifies the assets whose risks are assessed.
Knowing which components exist is a precondition for applying logical access protections to them.

controls.name: Data Classification
controls.summary: Classify data by sensitivity under a defined scheme with handling rules, and record the classification of each data store.
controls.statement: Maintain a data classification scheme defining {{ classification_levels }} and the handling requirements for each level, including storage, sharing, encryption, and retention. Record the classification of each in-scope data store in the component inventory, have {{ classification_approver }} approve classifications, and review the scheme and recorded classifications {{ classification_review_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Confidential and customer data can be located and is handled according to its sensitivity.
controls.guidance: Three or four levels are typical, such as public, internal, confidential, and restricted, with customer data classified confidential or higher. Tag cloud data stores and buckets with their level so automated checks can enforce encryption and access rules. Evidence: the scheme, the inventory showing classifications, and the review record.

mappings.summary: Classifying information and data stores overlaps with system and information categorization; impact-level categorization and authorizing official approval are not provided.
Classification identifies confidential information so it can be protected.
Classification informs which protections apply to each data store.

controls.name: Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plan
controls.summary: Maintain an approved business continuity and disaster recovery plan that defines recovery objectives, priorities, roles, and procedures, and keep it current.
controls.statement: Maintain a documented business continuity and disaster recovery plan, approved by {{ plan_approver }}, that identifies critical services with their recovery time and recovery point objectives, recovery priorities, contingency roles with current contact information, and procedures for continuing operations during a disruption and fully restoring systems afterward; review and update the plan {{ plan_review_cadence }} and after significant changes or tests, and communicate changes to {{ plan_recipients }}.
controls.objective: Ensure the organization can sustain critical services and restore systems to normal operation within committed timeframes after a disruption.
controls.guidance: Cover cloud-relevant scenarios such as availability zone and region outages, cloud account compromise or ransomware, loss of a critical SaaS dependency (identity provider, code hosting, payment processor), and loss of key personnel. Derive recovery objectives from the business impact analysis (OGRL-BC-07) and customer SLAs. Keep a copy accessible outside the primary environment in case SSO or the main workspace is unavailable, and restrict edit access. Align with the incident response plan (OGRL-IR-01) and fold in lessons from plan tests (OGRL-BC-02).

plan_recipients.label: Recipients of plan changes
plan_recipients.value: key contingency personnel and critical service owners

mappings.summary: The plan identifies critical functions, recovery objectives and priorities, roles, continuity and restoration procedures, and approval, but does not address sharing of contingency information.
Periodic plan review satisfies CP-2(d).
Updating the plan after significant changes and tests satisfies CP-2(e).
Communicating plan changes to key contingency personnel satisfies CP-2(f).
The plan defines the recovery objectives and procedures that recovery infrastructure is designed to meet.
Documented recovery procedures and priorities guide restoration after incidents.
A continuity plan is a primary risk mitigation activity for potential business disruptions.

controls.name: Continuity and Recovery Plan Testing
controls.summary: Exercise the business continuity and disaster recovery plan on a schedule, review results against recovery objectives, and remediate gaps.
controls.statement: Test the business continuity and disaster recovery plan {{ dr_test_cadence }} using {{ dr_test_methods }}, document results against recovery time and recovery point objectives, have results reviewed by {{ dr_test_reviewer }}, and track identified gaps to remediation.
controls.objective: Demonstrate that recovery procedures work and objectives are achievable, and correct weaknesses before a real disruption.
controls.guidance: Combine a tabletop walkthrough with a technical exercise such as promoting a database replica in another region or rebuilding an environment from infrastructure as code into a clean account. Measure actual recovery time and data loss and compare them with stated objectives. Tests may share a session with incident response tabletops (OGRL-IR-01) but keep separate results records. Feed findings back into the plan (OGRL-BC-01).

dr_test_methods.label: Plan test methods
dr_test_methods.value: a tabletop walkthrough and a technical failover or restoration exercise for at least one critical service

mappings.summary: Scheduled plan testing with defined methods, results review, and gap remediation satisfies CP-4 in full.
Exercising the continuity and recovery plan is the plan-level portion of recovery testing; backup restoration testing is a separate control.

controls.name: Data Backup
controls.summary: Back up production data and system state automatically, protect backups from tampering and loss, and alert on failures.
controls.statement: Back up {{ backup_scope }} {{ backup_frequency }} using automated backup jobs, encrypt backups, keep at least one copy in {{ backup_storage_location }} that production credentials cannot modify or delete, retain backups for {{ backup_retention }}, and alert {{ backup_alert_recipients }} when a backup job fails.
controls.objective: Ensure data and system state can be recovered after accidental deletion, corruption, ransomware, or infrastructure loss.
controls.guidance: Use managed snapshots and point-in-time recovery for databases and a central backup service with vault lock or object lock for immutability. Copy backups to a separate cloud account to isolate them from a compromised production account. Infrastructure as code and application source held in a hosted version control system count as system-level backups if the provider retains history. Periodically compare the backup inventory against the data store inventory to catch unprotected stores, and consider backups of critical SaaS data such as the document workspace.

backup_scope.label: Data and system state to back up
backup_scope.value: production databases, object storage, and system configuration not reproducible from version control

backup_storage_location.label: Isolated backup location
backup_storage_location.value: a separate cloud account or region

mappings.summary: Encrypting backups and isolating a copy from production credentials protects backup confidentiality at storage locations, alongside availability goals beyond 3.8.9.
Automated backups of production data stores at a defined frequency satisfy CP-9(a).
Backing up system configuration and state not held in version control at the same frequency satisfies CP-9(b).
Encryption, immutable isolated copies, and failure alerting protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of backups per CP-9(d).
Automated, protected backups are a core element of the data backup processes this criterion addresses.
Backups provide the data needed to restore systems when recovering from incidents.

controls.name: Backup Restoration Testing
controls.summary: Periodically restore backups of critical data stores to confirm they are usable, complete, and recoverable within objectives.
controls.statement: Restore backups of each critical data store {{ restore_test_cadence }} into an isolated environment, verify data completeness and integrity against defined checks, record the restore duration and data recency against recovery time and recovery point objectives, and remediate failed tests.
controls.objective: Confirm that backups are reliable and can be restored within committed recovery objectives before they are needed.
controls.guidance: Automate restore tests where possible, for example a scheduled job that restores the latest snapshot to a temporary instance, runs row-count and checksum queries, records timing, and tears down the instance. Rotate which data stores are tested if full coverage each period is impractical, but test every critical store at least annually. Keep the job output or a ticket per test as evidence.

mappings.summary: Scheduled restore tests with completeness and integrity checks verify backup reliability and integrity per CP-9(1).
Restore testing confirms that backup processes actually support recovery.
Backup restoration tests are one part of testing recovery procedures.

controls.name: Redundant Processing and Storage Sites
controls.summary: Run critical services across redundant locations, keep backups in a separate region, and secure alternate locations to the same baseline as primary.
controls.statement: Run critical production services across {{ processing_redundancy }} with the ability to resume them at an alternate processing location within {{ failover_time_limit }}, keep backup copies in {{ alternate_storage_location }}, and apply the same security baseline to alternate locations as to the primary environment.
controls.objective: Ensure the loss of a single facility, zone, or region does not cause prolonged unavailability or loss of data.
controls.guidance: In cloud environments, alternate sites are additional availability zones and regions rather than separate data centers, and provider agreements cover the facilities. Deploy stateless tiers across zones behind load balancers and use multi-zone managed databases. For regional failover, keep infrastructure as code and container images deployable to a secondary region and replicate backups there. Apply identical IaC modules, IAM guardrails, logging, and encryption settings to every region so the secondary environment is not a weaker target.

alternate_storage_location.label: Alternate storage location
alternate_storage_location.value: a region geographically separate from the primary data

failover_time_limit.label: Alternate processing resumption time
failover_time_limit.value: the recovery time objective defined in the business continuity plan

mappings.summary: Storing backups in a separate region with an equivalent security baseline establishes an alternate storage site per CP-6.
Multi-zone deployment with the ability to resume at an alternate location within a defined time establishes an alternate processing capability per CP-7(a).
Applying the same security baseline to alternate locations satisfies CP-7(c).
Redundant processing and storage locations are recovery infrastructure within this criterion.

controls.name: System Recovery and Reconstitution
controls.summary: Restore affected systems to a known-good, secure state within defined recovery time and recovery point objectives after a disruption.
controls.statement: After a disruption, compromise, or failure, recover affected systems to a known-good state within {{ recovery_time_objective }} and with data loss no greater than {{ recovery_point_objective }} using documented recovery runbooks and infrastructure as code, and verify that security configurations and controls are restored and functioning before returning systems to service.
controls.objective: Return systems to normal, secure operation within committed timeframes and without degrading the controls that protect them.
controls.guidance: Rebuild from infrastructure as code and trusted images rather than patching compromised hosts in place. Restore data from the most recent clean backup, which may predate the latest backup after ransomware or corruption. Use a recovery checklist that confirms logging, encryption, access policies, and monitoring are active before reopening traffic. Tighten the default objectives per service based on the business impact analysis (OGRL-BC-07). Evidence is the recovery record showing timing and the completed checklist.

mappings.summary: Recovering to a known-good state within defined recovery objectives satisfies CP-10.
Runbook-driven restoration within objectives relies on and exercises the recovery infrastructure.
Restoring systems to a secure state is the recovery activity following an incident.

controls.name: Business Impact Analysis
controls.summary: Analyze the impact of disruption to critical business functions and the systems and dependencies that support them to set recovery objectives.
controls.statement: Perform a business impact analysis {{ bia_cadence }} and upon significant changes to services or infrastructure that identifies critical business functions and the systems, data, personnel, and third-party dependencies supporting them, rates their criticality, and determines the maximum tolerable downtime and data loss used to set recovery objectives.
controls.objective: Ensure recovery priorities and objectives reflect the actual impact of disruption on customers and the business.
controls.guidance: Keep the analysis lightweight: a table of customer-facing services and internal functions with their supporting cloud resources, data stores, and SaaS vendors, a criticality tier, impact over time (for example at 1 hour, 1 day, 1 week), and the resulting recovery objectives. Draw dependencies from the system inventory (OGRL-AM-01) and vendor inventory (OGRL-TP-01). Feed results into the continuity plan (OGRL-BC-01).

mappings.summary: The analysis identifies the critical system assets supporting essential business functions as CP-2(8) requires.
Rating the criticality of supporting systems and dependencies overlaps criticality analysis, though not performed at system development decision points.
Impact analysis sets the recovery objectives that backup and recovery infrastructure must support.
Understanding the impact of disruption informs selection of business disruption risk mitigation activities.

controls.name: Capacity Planning and Monitoring
controls.summary: Monitor resource utilization and quotas against thresholds and periodically forecast capacity needs, including for contingency operations.
controls.statement: Monitor utilization of critical compute, storage, database, and network resources and cloud service quotas, alert {{ capacity_alert_recipients }} when utilization exceeds {{ capacity_alert_threshold }}, and review capacity forecasts {{ capacity_review_cadence }} to provision additional capacity, including the capacity needed to operate from alternate locations during contingency operations.
controls.objective: Maintain sufficient capacity to meet availability commitments as demand grows and during failover.
controls.guidance: Use cloud-native metrics and alarms for CPU, memory, disk, connection counts, queue depth, and service quota usage, and enable autoscaling with sensible maximums. Confirm that quotas and reserved capacity in the failover region can absorb production load. Record capacity reviews in a recurring ticket or meeting notes with resulting actions.

capacity_alert_threshold.label: Capacity alert threshold
capacity_alert_threshold.value: 80 percent of provisioned capacity or quota

mappings.summary: Capacity forecasting explicitly includes contingency operations, covering CP-2(2), and adds ongoing utilization monitoring and alerting.
Utilization monitoring and capacity forecasting are central to managing processing capacity for availability.

controls.name: Denial-of-Service Protection
controls.summary: Protect internet-facing services against denial-of-service attacks with layered mitigations and alerting.
controls.statement: Protect internet-facing services against the effects of {{ dos_event_types }} by employing {{ dos_protections }} in front of all public endpoints, and alert {{ dos_alert_recipients }} when attack traffic or rate-limit thresholds are exceeded.
controls.objective: Keep services available to legitimate users during denial-of-service attacks.
controls.guidance: Place public endpoints behind a CDN or cloud load balancer with provider DDoS protection, add WAF rate-based rules for login, signup, and expensive API routes, and apply per-tenant or per-key API quotas. Avoid exposing origin servers directly. Keep a runbook for engaging the provider's DDoS response team during large attacks.

dos_event_types.label: Denial-of-service event types
dos_event_types.value: volumetric network floods, protocol attacks, and application-layer request floods

dos_protections.label: Denial-of-service protections
dos_protections.value: cloud DDoS mitigation, web application firewall rate limiting, and API request quotas

mappings.summary: Layered denial-of-service mitigations for defined attack types satisfy SC-5.
DoS protection preserves usable capacity under attack traffic, complementing capacity management.
DoS mitigation at public endpoints is a boundary protection against threats from outside the system.

controls.name: Peer-Reviewed Production Change Control
controls.summary: Require independent peer review, automated testing, and traceable approval before deploying production code or infrastructure changes.
controls.statement: Require independent peer review, automated verification checks, and documented approval overseen by {{ change_authority }} before merging or deploying changes to production, retaining change records for {{ change_record_retention }}.
controls.objective: Prevent unauthorized, untested, or unreviewed modifications to production code and infrastructure.
controls.guidance: Enforce branch protection rules that prevent self-approval, require passing CI checks, and link deployments to immutable commit hashes and review tickets.

change_authority.label: Change oversight authority
change_authority.value: designated code owners and the change advisory workflow

tests.name: Verify Branch Protection and Peer-Reviewed Deployments
tests.description: Confirm production repositories enforce required independent pull-request reviews and passing CI status checks with no bypassed merges.

mappings.summary: Peer-reviewed production change control satisfies ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.32.
Production changes are tracked, peer reviewed, approved, and retained as records; changes made outside the code and deployment pipeline, such as endpoint or SaaS settings, are not covered.
Peer-reviewed change authorization and tracking satisfy SP 800-171 03.04.03.
Retaining pull-request review and deployment audit trails satisfies NIST CM-3(e).
Change oversight through code owners and change advisory workflows satisfies NIST CM-3(g).
Peer-reviewed and CI-verified production change control directly satisfies SOC 2 CC8.1.

controls.name: Baseline Configuration and Hardening Standards
controls.summary: Define hardened, version-controlled configuration baselines for in-scope components and build new components only from them.
controls.statement: Define hardened baseline configurations for {{ baseline_scope }} derived from {{ hardening_benchmark }}, maintain them as version-controlled code or templates, provision new components only from an approved baseline, require documented approval by {{ deviation_approver }} for any deviation, and review and update each baseline {{ baseline_review_frequency }} and whenever covered components are introduced or upgraded.
controls.objective: Ensure in-scope components start from, and remain traceable to, an approved secure configuration rather than ad hoc vendor defaults.
controls.guidance: Express baselines as infrastructure-as-code modules, golden machine images, hardened container base images, and organization-level cloud policies (for example AWS SCPs, Azure Policy, or GCP organization policies). Keep a short deviation register linked to the baseline repository. Use CIS Benchmarks or provider security best-practice guides as the starting point and record which settings were tailored and why. Drift detection against these baselines is covered by OGRL-CM-03.

baseline_scope.label: Components covered by hardened baselines
baseline_scope.value: cloud accounts and projects, compute images, container base images, managed databases, and network configurations

hardening_benchmark.label: Hardening benchmark source
hardening_benchmark.value: CIS Benchmarks or the cloud provider's security best-practice guidance

mappings.summary: Establishes and periodically reviews hardened baseline configurations; the system inventory and explicit coverage of hardware, firmware, and documentation are not addressed.
Defines benchmark-derived security settings in the baseline and builds components only from it; ongoing enforcement after deployment relies on drift control elsewhere.
Version-controlled hardened baselines satisfy the CM-2(a) obligation to develop, document, and maintain a baseline under configuration control.
The periodic baseline review supplies the CM-2(b)(1) review frequency.
Baselines are reviewed and updated whenever covered components are introduced or upgraded, as CM-2(b)(3) requires.
Baselines derived from a named hardening benchmark establish restrictive configuration settings per CM-6(a).
Provisioning only from approved baselines implements the documented configuration settings per CM-6(b).
Documented, approved baseline deviations for in-scope components address CM-6(c).
Hardened baselines are a technology general control contributing to CC5.2.
Defined secure configuration standards are one input to the configuration and vulnerability monitoring expected under CC7.1.

controls.name: Configuration Drift Detection
controls.summary: Automatically detect production configuration that diverges from the approved baseline and resolve each drift.
controls.statement: Continuously compare the running configuration of {{ drift_scope }} against its approved baseline using {{ drift_detection_tooling }}, alert {{ drift_alert_recipients }} on unapproved deviations, and revert or formally approve each detected drift within {{ drift_remediation_sla }}.
controls.objective: Detect unauthorized or accidental configuration changes quickly so production does not silently diverge from its approved secure state.
controls.guidance: Run scheduled infrastructure-as-code plan or drift checks (for example terraform plan in CI, AWS Config, or Azure Policy compliance) and a CSPM tool against production accounts. Route findings to the owning team's queue with the SLA as a due date. Evidence is the drift tool configuration plus a sample of alerts showing revert or approval within SLA.

drift_alert_recipients.label: Drift alert recipients
drift_alert_recipients.value: the owning engineering team and the security team

drift_detection_tooling.label: Drift detection mechanisms
drift_detection_tooling.value: automated infrastructure-as-code drift checks and cloud security posture management (CSPM) rules

drift_remediation_sla.label: Drift resolution SLA
drift_remediation_sla.value: 7 days for security-relevant settings and 30 days for all other settings

drift_scope.label: Components monitored for drift
drift_scope.value: production cloud resources and infrastructure-as-code managed components

mappings.summary: Enforces approved configuration settings by detecting and correcting drift; defining the settings and coverage beyond production cloud resources are not addressed.
Automated drift checks keep the recorded baseline and actual state aligned, partly supporting CM-2(2) accuracy and currency.
Drift tooling provides the automated verification element of CM-6(1); central management and application are covered elsewhere.
Automated drift detection and resolution monitors and controls changes to configuration settings under CM-6(d).
Detecting configuration changes that depart from approved baselines is a monitoring activity within CC7.1.
Drift detection surfaces changes made outside the authorized change process, supporting CC8.1.

controls.name: Security Impact Analysis of Changes
controls.summary: Analyze and sign off on the security and privacy impact of significant changes before they are deployed.
controls.statement: Before implementing {{ significant_change_types }}, document an analysis of the change's potential security and privacy impact, covering affected data, trust boundaries, access paths, and existing controls, and obtain sign-off from {{ impact_reviewer }} prior to deployment.
controls.objective: Ensure significant changes do not introduce unassessed security or privacy risk into production.
controls.guidance: Add a security-impact section to the design document or pull-request template that is required when a change matches a significant-change label. Lightweight threat modeling (for example STRIDE on a data-flow diagram) is sufficient for most changes. Organization-level risk re-evaluation for significant business changes is covered by the risk family.

impact_reviewer.label: Security impact sign-off authority
impact_reviewer.value: the security lead or a designated security reviewer

significant_change_types.label: Changes requiring security impact analysis
significant_change_types.value: significant changes, including new external integrations, changes to authentication or authorization, new data stores holding customer data, and network boundary changes

mappings.summary: Documented security impact analysis with sign-off before deployment meets 3.4.4 when the defined change types include all changes to CUI systems.
Pre-deployment security and privacy impact analysis for significant changes covers CM-4 for that subset of changes.
Analyzing the security impact of significant system changes partly addresses identifying risks from change under CC3.4.
Security impact analysis of significant changes is part of designing and authorizing changes under CC8.1.

controls.name: Production Change Access Restrictions
controls.summary: Limit who and what can change production to the deployment pipeline and a small reviewed set of identities.
controls.statement: Restrict permissions to deploy to or modify production systems to {{ deploy_authorized_identities }} acting through the CI/CD pipeline or infrastructure-as-code workflow, prohibit direct manual changes outside that path except under the emergency change procedure, and review the identities holding production change permissions {{ change_access_review_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Ensure production can only be changed through the controlled, reviewable delivery path.
controls.guidance: Grant production write access to the pipeline's workload identity (for example GitHub Actions OIDC roles) rather than to humans. Keep human production access read-only by default with just-in-time elevation. Use GitHub environments with required reviewers and restrict who can modify pipeline definitions. Evidence is the IAM policy export and the quarterly review record.

deploy_authorized_identities.label: Identities permitted to change production
deploy_authorized_identities.value: the automated deployment pipeline and a named set of platform engineers

mappings.summary: Defines and enforces logical restrictions on who can change production and reviews them; physical change restrictions and formal approval of the restrictions are not addressed.
Defines and enforces logical access restrictions for changing production; physical change restrictions are out of scope.
Limiting production change permissions is a logical access restriction over protected assets under CC6.1.
Restricting who can implement production changes supports the authorized change process under CC8.1.

controls.name: Emergency Change Procedure
controls.summary: Allow expedited production changes during incidents while preserving authorization, records, and after-the-fact review.
controls.statement: Permit changes that bypass standard pre-deployment approval only when authorized by {{ emergency_authorizer }} to resolve an active incident or critical vulnerability, record each emergency change with its justification and linked incident or ticket, and complete retrospective peer review and approval of the change within {{ retro_review_window }}.
controls.objective: Allow rapid remediation without creating an unreviewed path into production.
controls.guidance: Use a dedicated emergency label or break-glass deployment workflow that records who invoked it and requires an incident ID. A weekly query for merges that bypassed branch protection or deployments without an approved review gives auditors a complete population to sample.

emergency_authorizer.label: Emergency change authorizer
emergency_authorizer.value: the incident commander or on-call engineering lead

mappings.summary: Emergency changes receive authorization and retrospective review, a variant of CM-3(b) approval for the expedited path.
Recording each emergency change with its justification documents change decisions for that class of change under CM-3(c).
An authorized, documented, and retrospectively reviewed emergency path is part of change management under CC8.1.

controls.name: Change Testing and Environment Separation
controls.summary: Test changes in separated non-production environments with automated gates before production deployment.
controls.statement: Test and validate each change in {{ test_environment }} that is logically separated from production before deployment, require automated test suites to pass as a merge or deployment gate, retain test results with the change record, and prohibit unmasked production customer data in non-production environments unless approved by {{ prod_data_exception_approver }}.
controls.objective: Catch defects and unintended effects before they reach production without exposing customer data in lower environments.
controls.guidance: Run staging in a separate cloud account or project with distinct credentials. Configure required status checks in branch protection so merges are blocked on failing tests, and keep CI run links on the pull request. Use synthetic or masked data sets for testing.

prod_data_exception_approver.label: Production data in test exception approver

test_environment.label: Pre-production test environment
test_environment.value: a staging environment in a separate cloud account or project

mappings.summary: Gated testing, validation, and retained results before deployment meet CM-3(2).
Changes are exercised in a separate test environment, though analysis is not necessarily focused on security and privacy impact as CM-4(1) expects.
Pre-production testing in separated environments is part of the change process under CC8.1.

controls.name: Least Functionality and Software Restriction
controls.summary: Run only required services and ports on production, and restrict software installation to approved sources.
controls.statement: Configure production hosts and container images to run only the services, ports, and protocols required for their function with all others disabled or blocked by default, restrict software installation on production systems and workforce endpoints to {{ approved_software_sources }} enforced through {{ software_enforcement_methods }}, and review compliance {{ software_compliance_review_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Reduce attack surface and prevent unauthorized or malicious software from being introduced.
controls.guidance: Use minimal or distroless base images, default-deny security groups, and read-only root filesystems. On endpoints, remove local administrator rights and use MDM-managed application catalogs or allow-listing. A quarterly export of listening ports, image package lists, and MDM installed-software reports provides evidence.

approved_software_sources.label: Approved software sources
approved_software_sources.value: approved package repositories, the internal container registry, and the MDM-managed software catalog

software_enforcement_methods.label: Software restriction enforcement methods
software_enforcement_methods.value: immutable container images, removal of local administrator rights, and MDM application allow-listing

mappings.summary: Configures production hosts and images to run only required services, ports, and protocols; documenting essential capabilities and covering endpoints and network devices are not addressed.
Disables nonessential services, ports, and protocols on production hosts and restricts software sources; explicit definition of essential programs and functions and endpoint coverage are missing.

Restricting software to approved sources with MDM allow-listing contributes to an allow-list policy, but the policy choice, authorized software list, and execution control on all CUI endpoints are not specified.
Removing local administrator rights and limiting installs to approved sources controls user-installed software; continuous monitoring of installations is weaker than periodic compliance review.
Named enforcement methods for software installation satisfy CM-11(b).
Periodic compliance review supplies the CM-11(c) monitoring frequency.
Running only required services, ports, and protocols provides only essential capabilities per CM-7(a).
Default-deny of unneeded services and restricted software sources overlap with the CM-7(b) prohibitions, which the organization still enumerates.
Restricting software installation and unneeded functionality helps prevent unauthorized software under CC6.8.

controls.name: Software and Data Integrity Verification
controls.summary: Verify the integrity of build artifacts and critical system files and act on unauthorized changes.
controls.statement: Verify the integrity of {{ integrity_protected_assets }} using {{ integrity_mechanisms }} before deployment and while running, and when verification fails or an unauthorized change is detected, {{ integrity_response_actions }}.
