controls.objective: Detect and stop tampered or unauthorized software and configuration before it can affect production.
controls.guidance: Sign build artifacts and container images in CI (for example Sigstore cosign), pin deployments to image digests, and enforce signature verification with an admission controller or deployment policy. Use file integrity monitoring or immutable infrastructure for hosts. Integrity of customer data stores is addressed by the data integrity control in the cryptography family.

integrity_mechanisms.label: Integrity verification mechanisms
integrity_mechanisms.value: cryptographic signing and digest pinning of artifacts and images, plus file integrity monitoring on hosts

integrity_protected_assets.label: Assets subject to integrity verification
integrity_protected_assets.value: build artifacts, container images, infrastructure-as-code templates, and critical system binaries and configuration files

integrity_response_actions.label: Actions on integrity failure
integrity_response_actions.value: block the deployment or isolate the affected host, alert the security on-call team, and open a security incident

mappings.summary: Integrity verification covers software and critical configuration; firmware and general information are out of scope for SI-7(a).
Defined response actions on integrity failure satisfy SI-7(b).
Blocking unsigned or tampered software helps prevent unauthorized or malicious software under CC6.8.

controls.name: System Maintenance and Maintenance Tool Control
controls.summary: Perform scheduled, approved, and recorded maintenance on in-scope components using only approved tools, techniques, and personnel.
controls.statement: Perform maintenance, repair, and replacement of {{ maintenance_scope }} on a documented schedule based on manufacturer or vendor specifications and organizational requirements; approve and monitor all maintenance, requiring approval by {{ maintenance_approver }} before any maintenance activity not covered by a pre-approved standard maintenance procedure, whether performed on site, remotely, or with components removed off site; allow maintenance to be performed only by {{ authorized_maintenance_personnel }} using the techniques set out in documented maintenance procedures; permit only the maintenance tools and mechanisms listed in an approved maintenance tool register, restrict access to those tools to authorized maintenance personnel, and monitor their use through maintenance records and tool logs; record {{ maintenance_record_contents }} for each maintenance activity and review the records {{ maintenance_record_review_frequency }}; and review the maintenance tool register {{ maintenance_tool_review_frequency }}, removing tools that are no longer needed or supported.
controls.objective: Keep in-scope systems in a serviceable, supported condition through maintenance that is planned, authorized, and traceable, and prevent maintenance tools, techniques, and personnel from becoming an uncontrolled path into the system.
controls.guidance: For cloud and SaaS services, physical maintenance of provider hardware is inherited from the provider (for CUI, a FedRAMP Moderate or equivalent offering); record the inheritance in the system security plan and customer responsibility matrix. This control then covers organization-managed workforce endpoints, network and security appliances, on-premises servers, and the organization's own maintenance of cloud workloads such as OS patch windows and managed database maintenance windows. Routine work such as the monthly patch window or MDM-driven updates can be approved once as a standard maintenance procedure and evidenced by tickets or RMM and MDM logs; break-fix work, vendor visits, and remote vendor support need individual approval. The maintenance tool register lists hardware diagnostic utilities, firmware update tools, remote support and RMM agents (including those operated by a managed service provider), and administrative consoles or scripts used for maintenance; it can live alongside the software inventory. Patching is covered by OGRL-VM-02, off-site sanitization by OGRL-CM-11, diagnostic media by OGRL-CM-12, remote maintenance sessions by OGRL-CM-13, maintenance personnel supervision by OGRL-CM-14, and facility infrastructure maintenance by OGRL-PS-07.

authorized_maintenance_personnel.label: Personnel permitted to perform maintenance
authorized_maintenance_personnel.value: workforce members assigned maintenance responsibilities and vendor personnel on the authorized maintenance list, with any other personnel escorted and supervised

maintenance_approver.label: Maintenance approval authority
maintenance_approver.value: the system owner or IT lead

maintenance_record_contents.label: Required maintenance record contents
maintenance_record_contents.value: date and time, component, maintenance performed, tools used, personnel performing the work, approver, and any components removed or replaced

maintenance_scope.label: Components subject to controlled maintenance
maintenance_scope.value: system components that process, store, or transmit CUI or provide security protection for them, including workforce endpoints, network and security appliances, and organization-managed servers and cloud workloads

mappings.summary: Scheduled, approved, and recorded maintenance of in-scope components performs system maintenance, and the control adds tool and personnel restrictions beyond 3.7.1.

An approved tool register, documented maintenance procedures, and restriction to authorized personnel control the tools, techniques, mechanisms, and personnel used for maintenance, alongside scheduling and record-keeping that 3.7.2 does not require.
Scheduled maintenance per vendor specifications with recorded and periodically reviewed maintenance records meets MA-2(a).
Approval and monitoring of every maintenance activity, whether on site, remote, or off site, meets MA-2(b).
A defined set of maintenance record contents is captured for every maintenance activity, as MA-2(f) requires.
Only tools in an approved register may be used, access to them is restricted, and their use is monitored, meeting MA-3(a).
The approved maintenance tool register is reviewed on a set cadence, meeting MA-3(b).

controls.name: Off-Site Maintenance Equipment Sanitization
controls.summary: Sanitize or remove storage media of any equipment before it leaves for off-site maintenance and record the result.
controls.statement: Before {{ offsite_equipment_types }} leave organizational control for off-site maintenance, repair, warranty replacement, or vendor depot service, sanitize all associated storage media of {{ offsite_sanitization_information }} using {{ offsite_sanitization_method }}, or remove the storage media and retain it under organizational control; keep equipment that can be neither sanitized nor separated from its storage media in organizational custody; and, before release, record the asset identifier, sanitization method or media removal, performer, verification result, and receiving party in the maintenance record.
controls.objective: Ensure no CUI leaves organizational control on equipment sent out for maintenance, repair, or replacement.
controls.guidance: The common cases for a small contractor are a laptop shipped to the manufacturer's depot for warranty repair, a phone swapped by a carrier, and a multifunction printer or network appliance collected by a vendor. Where devices use FIPS-validated full-disk encryption (OGRL-CR-06), an MDM remote wipe that performs a cryptographic erase is usually the quickest acceptable method; verify the result in the MDM console and record it. If a failed device cannot be wiped, remove and keep the drive, buy the manufacturer's keep-your-drive option, arrange on-site repair under supervision (OGRL-CM-14), or retire the device through OGRL-CR-04 instead of shipping it. Reimage returned equipment from the approved baseline (OGRL-CM-02) before reconnecting it. Approval to send equipment off site is part of OGRL-CM-10, and end-of-life disposal is OGRL-CR-04. Hardware maintenance inside a cloud provider's data centers is inherited from the provider's FedRAMP or equivalent authorization.

offsite_equipment_types.label: Equipment subject to sanitization before off-site maintenance
offsite_equipment_types.value: workforce laptops and desktops, mobile devices, removable storage, printers and multifunction devices with internal storage, and servers, storage arrays, or network appliances that have processed, stored, or transmitted CUI

offsite_sanitization_information.label: Information removed before equipment leaves for maintenance
offsite_sanitization_information.value: all CUI and other organizational information, including credentials, keys, configuration files, and cached authentication material

offsite_sanitization_method.label: Sanitization method for equipment sent off site
offsite_sanitization_method.value: NIST SP 800-88 clear or purge techniques appropriate to the media, such as a cryptographic erase of FIPS-validated full-disk-encrypted storage, a vendor secure-erase command, or overwriting, followed by verification

mappings.summary: Equipment leaving for off-site maintenance is sanitized of CUI or has its storage media removed, as 3.7.3 requires.
Storage media is sanitized of defined information, or removed, before equipment leaves for off-site maintenance, meeting MA-2(d).

controls.name: Diagnostic Media Malware Inspection
controls.summary: Scan diagnostic and test media for malware before it is used on systems that handle CUI.
controls.statement: Before {{ diagnostic_media_types }} are used on systems that process, store, or transmit CUI, scan the media and its contents for malicious code using {{ media_scanning_mechanism }} with current detection signatures, verify the publisher's digital signature or published checksum where one is available, prohibit use of media that fails inspection or cannot be inspected, and record the inspection result in the maintenance record.
controls.objective: Prevent media brought in for diagnostics or testing from introducing malicious code into systems that handle CUI.
controls.guidance: Typical triggers are a field engineer arriving with a USB drive of diagnostics, firmware update media for a firewall or switch, and manufacturer diagnostic utilities or boot images downloaded for a failing laptop. A small contractor can keep one designated scanning workstation (a managed machine outside the CUI enclave, with current anti-malware definitions) and require all such media to pass through it; scan the technician's media before the visit starts. For downloaded tools, check the publisher's signature or published hash, and prefer distributing them through the managed software catalog so endpoint protection inspects them. If removable media is blocked on CUI systems (OGRL-PS-08) and diagnostic tools come only from vendor repositories through managed distribution, document that as the inspection mechanism. Malware protection itself is OGRL-VM-03.

diagnostic_media_types.label: Media subject to inspection before use
diagnostic_media_types.value: media containing diagnostic, test, or firmware update programs, including vendor- or technician-supplied USB drives and optical discs, bootable diagnostic media, and downloaded diagnostic utilities and images

media_scanning_mechanism.label: Mechanism used to inspect diagnostic media
media_scanning_mechanism.value: the organization's managed anti-malware engine on a designated scanning workstation that is not connected to CUI systems

mappings.summary: Media with diagnostic and test programs is scanned for malicious code before use on CUI systems, as 3.7.4 requires.
Diagnostic and test media is scanned for malicious code before use, meeting MA-3(2).

controls.name: Nonlocal Maintenance Session Controls
controls.summary: Run remote maintenance only through approved, MFA-protected, logged tools and close each session when the work is done.
controls.statement: Allow nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions to {{ nonlocal_maintenance_scope }} only through {{ approved_nonlocal_maintenance_tools }} documented in the system security plan; approve nonlocal maintenance by granting it only to roles authorized for maintenance and requiring approval by {{ nonlocal_session_approver }} before each session initiated by external maintenance personnel; require multifactor authentication to establish every nonlocal maintenance session via an external network connection; log and monitor each session, recording the person, target system, purpose, and start and end times; and terminate the session and its network connections, and disable any access enabled for the session, when the maintenance is complete, with sessions automatically terminated after {{ nonlocal_session_idle_timeout }} of inactivity.
controls.objective: Ensure remote maintenance sessions are authorized, strongly authenticated, observable, and closed as soon as the work is done.
controls.guidance: Nonlocal maintenance is any maintenance or diagnostics performed by someone communicating over an external network: an MSP technician using an RMM agent, a vendor support engineer on a remote-control session (for example BeyondTrust, TeamViewer, or a screen-share with remote control), and administrators maintaining cloud workloads or SaaS tenants from the internet. Keep vendor accounts and unattended remote agents disabled by default and enable them just in time for an approved session. Enforce multifactor authentication on the session itself, through the identity provider (OGRL-AC-05) or the remote support tool's own MFA bound to the organization's tenant; a technician's MFA to their employer's portal plus a user clicking "allow" is weak evidence. Session logs from the tool, VPN, or cloud session manager can serve as the maintenance record; set idle and maximum session timeouts in the tool. General remote access is OGRL-AC-11; supervising unauthorized technicians is OGRL-CM-14.

approved_nonlocal_maintenance_tools.label: Approved nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic tools
approved_nonlocal_maintenance_tools.value: the organization's managed remote access VPN or zero-trust access service, cloud provider session management services, and an approved remote support tool that records sessions

nonlocal_maintenance_scope.label: Systems in scope for nonlocal maintenance controls
nonlocal_maintenance_scope.value: systems that process, store, or transmit CUI or provide security protection for them, including cloud and SaaS administrative consoles, servers, network appliances, and workforce endpoints

nonlocal_session_approver.label: Approver for sessions by external maintenance personnel
nonlocal_session_approver.value: the system owner or IT lead

nonlocal_session_idle_timeout.label: Inactivity period after which sessions are terminated

mappings.summary: Requires MFA to establish and termination to end nonlocal maintenance sessions, and additionally restricts tools, approves sessions, and logs them.
Nonlocal maintenance is limited to authorized roles, external sessions need per-session approval, and every session is monitored, meeting MA-4(a).
Nonlocal maintenance is allowed only through approved tools documented in the system security plan, meeting MA-4(b).
Multifactor authentication is required to establish every nonlocal maintenance session, meeting MA-4(c).
Each nonlocal maintenance session is logged with person, target, purpose, and timing, meeting MA-4(d).
Sessions, network connections, and session-specific access are terminated when nonlocal maintenance ends, meeting MA-4(e).

controls.name: Maintenance Personnel Supervision
controls.summary: Keep an authorized maintenance personnel list and escort and supervise anyone without CUI access authorization during maintenance.
controls.statement: Maintain a list of maintenance organizations and personnel authorized to perform maintenance on {{ maintenance_personnel_scope }}, approved by {{ maintenance_personnel_approver }} and reviewed {{ authorized_maintenance_list_review_frequency }}; before maintenance begins, verify that any personnel who will work unescorted are on the list and hold the access authorizations required for the systems and CUI involved; and ensure that maintenance by personnel without those authorizations is escorted and supervised for its full duration, on site or through an observed remote session, by {{ maintenance_supervisor }}, recording the supervisor in the maintenance record.
controls.objective: Ensure no one without the required access authorization performs maintenance on CUI systems unobserved.
controls.guidance: Typical cases are a copier technician, a manufacturer field engineer replacing a server part, an ISP installing network equipment, and an MSP or software vendor engineer on a remote session. Access authorization for CUI usually means a workforce member, or a vendor bound by contract (OGRL-HR-04), who has been screened (OGRL-HR-01) and signed access agreements (OGRL-HR-03). For on-site work by anyone else, the escort stays with them for the whole visit, CUI is removed, covered, or locked away and screens are locked where feasible, and the visit is logged (OGRL-PS-03). For remote work, the supervisor watches the full screen-share and is able to end it (OGRL-CM-13). The supervisor needs enough technical competence to recognize and stop actions outside the agreed scope. A short table in the maintenance procedure is enough for the authorized list.

maintenance_personnel_approver.label: Approver of authorized maintenance organizations and personnel
maintenance_personnel_approver.value: the IT lead or security lead

maintenance_personnel_scope.label: Systems covered by maintenance personnel authorization
maintenance_personnel_scope.value: systems that process, store, or transmit CUI or provide security protection for them

maintenance_supervisor.label: Supervisor of maintenance by unauthorized personnel
maintenance_supervisor.value: a designated workforce member who holds the required access authorizations and has the technical competence to understand and stop the maintenance being performed

mappings.summary: Escorts and supervises maintenance by personnel lacking access authorization, and additionally maintains the authorized maintenance list and verifies unescorted personnel.
An approved, periodically reviewed list of authorized maintenance organizations and personnel meets MA-5(a).
Unescorted maintenance personnel are checked against the list and required access authorizations before work starts, meeting MA-5(b).
A supervisor with the required authorizations and technical competence oversees maintenance by unauthorized personnel, meeting MA-5(c).

controls.name: Encryption in Transit and at Rest
controls.summary: Encrypt sensitive data in transit using modern TLS and at rest using strong managed cryptographic keys.
controls.statement: Protect {{ protected_data_scope }} in transit using {{ transit_cipher_suite }} and at rest using {{ rest_cipher_suite }} with centrally managed keys.
controls.objective: Preserve confidentiality and integrity of sensitive data across networks and storage media.
controls.guidance: Disable TLS versions below 1.2, enforce HSTS on public web endpoints, and enable cloud KMS encryption on all databases, object stores, and block volumes.

protected_data_scope.label: Protected data scope
protected_data_scope.value: all customer, authentication, and confidential organizational data

tests.name: Verify TLS in Transit and Storage Encryption at Rest
tests.description: Verify public endpoints enforce TLS 1.2+ and all production databases, object buckets, and volumes have encryption at rest enabled.

mappings.summary: Modern TLS and managed AES-256 storage encryption satisfy ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.24.
TLS for protected data in transit encrypts most remote access traffic, but the control neither identifies remote access mechanisms nor explicitly requires every remote access session to be encrypted.
At-rest encryption of protected data reaches mobile devices only implicitly; the control does not identify the mobile devices that handle CUI or require device-level encryption on them.
Mandatory TLS authenticates endpoints and protects session integrity, but session identifier handling and non-TLS session protocols are not addressed.
Encrypting protected data at rest with managed keys protects the confidentiality of CUI at rest when the protected data scope includes CUI, and also covers transit.
Mandatory TLS for protected data in transit prevents disclosure of CUI during transmission, provided the protected data scope includes CUI.
Modern TLS and storage encryption satisfy SP 800-171 03.13.08 data protection.
Enforcing AES-256 encryption at rest with managed keys protects stored data per SC-28.
Enforcing modern TLS protects confidentiality and integrity of transmitted information per SC-8.
Encryption at rest protects information assets as part of the logical access safeguards in CC6.1.
TLS in transit and encryption at rest satisfy SOC 2 CC6.7 transmission and data protection.

controls.name: Cryptographic Key Management
controls.summary: Manage encryption keys in a dedicated key management service with restricted access, periodic rotation, and logged administration.
controls.statement: Generate, store, and use cryptographic keys protecting {{ key_scope }} within {{ key_management_system }}, restrict key administration and key use to authorized roles through least-privilege policies, rotate keys {{ key_rotation_period }} and upon suspected compromise, and log all key administration actions.
controls.objective: Keep cryptographic keys confidential, available, and under authorized control throughout their lifecycle so that encryption remains effective.
controls.guidance: Use a cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault) with HSM-backed keys and enable automatic rotation for customer-managed keys. Separate key administrators from key users in IAM policy, require a waiting period before key deletion, and send KMS audit events to the central log store. Manage TLS certificates through a managed certificate service with automated renewal. Keep a key inventory recording owner and purpose, and never embed key material in source code or images (see OGRL-AC-06).

key_management_system.label: Key management system
key_management_system.value: a FIPS 140-validated cloud key management service or HSM

key_scope.label: Data and services protected by managed keys
key_scope.value: production data stores, backups, and TLS endpoints

mappings.summary: Keys are generated, stored, used, rotated, and access-restricted in a managed key service, establishing and managing keys for the cryptography in scope.
Centralized key generation, storage, access restriction, rotation, and logging establish and manage keys as SC-12 requires.
Protecting encryption keys is one element of the logical access security measures this criterion covers.

controls.name: Data Retention and Disposal
controls.summary: Define retention periods for each data category, enforce them, and dispose of data that has expired or that customers ask to delete.
controls.statement: Define retention periods for each category of customer, personal, and confidential data in a documented retention schedule; enforce them through automated deletion or lifecycle rules where technically feasible; delete customer data within {{ customer_deletion_window }} of contract termination or a verified deletion request; and verify {{ retention_review_cadence }} that data past its retention period has been disposed of.
controls.objective: Retain information only as long as required for business, legal, and contractual purposes and dispose of it securely afterward.
controls.guidance: Implement retention with object storage lifecycle policies, database TTL or scheduled purge jobs, and log-group retention settings. Document that deleted data persists in backups until they age out under OGRL-BC-03. Provide a legal-hold process that suspends deletion when required. Per-tenant encryption keys enable cryptographic erasure of a customer's data at offboarding. Keep deletion job output or tickets as evidence and provide deletion confirmations to customers on request.

mappings.summary: A documented and enforced retention schedule manages and retains information in line with legal, contractual, and operational requirements per SI-12.
Scheduled and request-driven deletion disposes of confidential information when it is no longer needed.
Logical data disposal contributes to removing the ability to recover data before assets are retired, though physical media handling is addressed elsewhere.
The retention schedule governs how long personal information is kept.

controls.name: Media Sanitization and Secure Disposal
controls.summary: Sanitize storage media before disposal or reuse and keep a record of each sanitized asset.
controls.statement: Sanitize {{ media_scope }} prior to disposal, reuse, or release outside organizational control using {{ sanitization_methods }}, and retain a record of each sanitized asset including its identifier, method used, date, and the person or vendor performing the sanitization.
controls.objective: Prevent recovery of confidential and personal information from retired, reassigned, or returned storage media.
controls.guidance: For laptops, rely on full-disk encryption plus an MDM-initiated wipe or cryptographic erase before reassignment, and use a certified IT asset disposition vendor that issues certificates of destruction for retired hardware. Data center media is usually sanitized by the cloud provider; treat it as a subservice organization responsibility and confirm it in their SOC 2 report. For cloud volumes and tenant data, deleting the encryption key renders data unrecoverable. Reconcile disposal records against the asset inventory (OGRL-AM-01).

media_scope.label: Media requiring sanitization
media_scope.value: laptops, workstations, removable media, and other devices that store organizational data

sanitization_methods.label: Sanitization techniques
sanitization_methods.value: NIST SP 800-88 purge or destroy techniques, including cryptographic erase of encrypted devices

mappings.summary: Media is sanitized or destroyed with SP 800-88 techniques before disposal, reuse, or release, provided the media scope includes paper CUI.
Sanitizing defined media with defined techniques before disposal, reuse, or release satisfies MP-6(a).
Using purge or destroy techniques aligned to SP 800-88 supports sanitization strength commensurate with data sensitivity, without formal categorization-based selection.
Media sanitization is one mechanism for disposing of confidential information.
Sanitizing media before disposal ensures data cannot be recovered from retired assets.
Media sanitization is one mechanism for securely disposing of personal information.

controls.name: Data Store Integrity and Replication
controls.summary: Protect production data stores with storage-level integrity checks and multi-zone replication, and alert on integrity or replication failures.
controls.statement: Configure production data stores holding {{ integrity_scope }} with storage-level integrity verification and replication across at least {{ replica_zone_count }} availability zones, and alert {{ integrity_alert_recipients }} when integrity errors, replication failures, or replication lag exceeding {{ replication_lag_threshold }} are detected.
controls.objective: Ensure stored data remains complete and accurate and survives the loss of a single storage component or zone without corruption or loss.
controls.guidance: Prefer managed data stores with built-in checksumming and synchronous replication (for example multi-AZ relational databases and object storage with checksums and versioning), enable page checksums where the engine supports them, and alert on replica lag and storage error metrics. Replication propagates logical corruption and accidental deletes, so it complements rather than replaces backups (OGRL-BC-03). Run periodic consistency checks or reconciliations on critical tables. Software and artifact integrity verification is covered by OGRL-CM-09.

mappings.summary: Replicated copies preserve data availability, overlapping with backup objectives, but replication is not a substitute for point-in-time backups.
Storage-level integrity verification covers the information portion of SI-7(a) but not software or firmware.
Alerting on detected data integrity errors is a response action for information integrity under SI-7(b).
Integrity verification and replication help keep stored data complete and accurate over time.

controls.name: FIPS-Validated Cryptography for CUI
controls.summary: Inventory where cryptography protects CUI and use only FIPS-validated modules running in approved mode for those uses.
controls.statement: Maintain an inventory of {{ cui_crypto_uses }}, recording for each use the cryptographic module, its CMVP certificate number, and the algorithms in use; protect the confidentiality of CUI in each of those uses only with cryptographic modules holding {{ fips_validation_standard }}, configured to operate in the module's validated approved mode and limited to {{ approved_algorithms }}; and review the inventory against the CMVP listing {{ crypto_inventory_review_cadence }} and whenever a cryptographic use is added or a module is changed.
controls.objective: Ensure the cryptography relied on to keep CUI confidential has been independently validated and is operating as validated.
controls.guidance: Validation belongs to the cryptographic module, not the algorithm: "AES-256" alone is not evidence. For each use, record the product, module name, version, and CMVP certificate number, and keep a screenshot or export showing FIPS mode is on. Common sources: Windows with the FIPS policy enabled and BitLocker, macOS FileVault (Apple corecrypto modules), FIPS-enabled Linux distributions, GovCloud or FIPS endpoints of cloud providers and their KMS HSMs, Microsoft 365 GCC High, FIPS-certified VPN appliances, and hardware-encrypted USB drives with their own certificates. SaaS that stores or transmits CUI must document its FIPS-validated modules (often via a FedRAMP Moderate package). Prefer modules with an active certificate; treat modules on the CMVP historical list as a documented risk decision and plan their replacement. Remote workers inherit this control through managed device and VPN configuration. Re-check the inventory when products are upgraded, because a new version may not be covered by the certificate.

approved_algorithms.label: Permitted algorithms and protocol configurations
approved_algorithms.value: FIPS-approved algorithms and key lengths, such as AES-128 or AES-256, and TLS 1.2 or higher restricted to FIPS-approved cipher suites

crypto_inventory_review_cadence.label: Frequency of reviewing the CUI cryptography inventory against the CMVP

cui_crypto_uses.label: Cryptographic uses that protect CUI confidentiality
cui_crypto_uses.value: encryption of CUI in transit, including remote access, VPN, TLS, and email; encryption of CUI at rest on endpoints, mobile devices, servers, cloud storage, backups, and removable media; and any other cryptography used to protect CUI confidentiality

fips_validation_standard.label: Required cryptographic module validation
fips_validation_standard.value: a FIPS 140-2 or FIPS 140-3 validation certificate listed by the NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP)

mappings.summary: Only CMVP-validated modules operating in approved mode protect CUI confidentiality, with an inventory that evidences it, satisfying 3.13.11.
The CUI cryptography inventory determines the cryptographic uses that SC-13(a) asks the organization to identify.
Each inventoried use must employ the defined type of cryptography, namely FIPS-validated modules in approved mode.

controls.name: Information Security Program and Policy Framework
controls.summary: Maintain an approved, published set of information security policies that is reviewed on a fixed cadence and after significant change.
controls.statement: Maintain a documented information security policy set that defines the security program's scope, policy owners, and roles and responsibilities. The policy set is approved by {{ policy_approver }}, published to all workforce members, stored in a repository where only policy owners can modify it, and reviewed and updated {{ policy_review_frequency }} and following {{ policy_review_triggers }}.
controls.objective: Security expectations are formally defined, approved by accountable leadership, available to everyone they apply to, and kept current.
controls.guidance: A startup can start with a top-level information security policy plus topic policies (access control, change management, incident response, vendor management, data handling) kept in a wiki or Git repository with change history. Record each review and approval with a dated sign-off or merge approval; auditors typically sample the approval record, the publication location, and the version history. Map each policy to the controls that implement it so gaps are visible.

policy_review_triggers.label: Events triggering out-of-cycle policy review
policy_review_triggers.value: significant organizational, regulatory, contractual, or system changes

mappings.summary: The approved policy set serves as the program plan and assigns roles, but does not itself describe every program management and common control.
Scheduled and event-driven policy review and update fulfils the plan review requirement.
Restricting policy modification to owners in a controlled repository protects the plan from unauthorized change.
Publishing policies to all workforce members is one form of internal communication of security responsibilities.
The policy framework establishes the control activities intended to reduce risk; selection against assessed risk is addressed by risk controls.
Approved and published policies are the vehicle through which control activities are deployed; implementing procedures sit in other controls.

controls.name: Security Leadership and Organizational Structure
controls.summary: Formally designate an accountable security leader and document security roles, reporting lines, and responsibilities.
controls.statement: Designate in writing a {{ security_leader_role }} who is accountable for the information security program and has the authority and resources to run it. Maintain an organizational chart showing reporting lines and a document of security roles and responsibilities, and review both {{ org_review_frequency }} and when leadership or structure changes.
controls.objective: Accountability for security is assigned to a named individual, and reporting lines and responsibilities are clear and current.
controls.guidance: In small companies the role is often held by the CTO or a head of security as a part-time responsibility; that is acceptable if the designation is written and the person has the authority to act. Keep the org chart in the HRIS so it stays current, and keep a RACI for security activities (policy ownership, access reviews, incident command, vendor reviews). Evidence: the designation memo or board resolution, the dated org chart, and the reviewed RACI.

org_review_frequency.label: Org chart and responsibilities review frequency

security_leader_role.label: Accountable security leader role
security_leader_role.value: security officer (for example CISO, head of security, or CTO)

mappings.summary: Written designation of an accountable security leader with authority and resources covers the appointment requirement; documented reporting lines add scope.
Documented reporting lines, security roles, and a designated leader address organizational structure and authority for security.
Assigning named accountability for the security program supports holding individuals accountable; performance enforcement is elsewhere.

controls.name: Board Oversight of Security and Risk
controls.summary: Security leadership briefs the board or its designated committee on security and risk on a fixed cadence, and oversight is recorded.
controls.statement: Security leadership briefs {{ oversight_body }} on the state of the security program {{ briefing_frequency }}, covering top risks and their treatment status, significant incidents, control assessment and audit results, and open deficiencies. The oversight body's review, questions, and decisions are recorded in meeting minutes.
controls.objective: Those charged with governance exercise informed, documented oversight of security and risk independently of the management that operates the controls.
controls.guidance: Pre-revenue companies with an informal board can use a board meeting agenda item with a short security deck; record attendance and decisions in minutes. Where the board includes outside or independent directors, note their participation. Auditors usually sample the deck and minutes for each briefing in the period.

oversight_body.label: Governance body exercising oversight
oversight_body.value: the board of directors or a designated board committee

mappings.summary: Documented board briefings demonstrate oversight of security; board independence and composition are outside this control.
Briefing the governing body is one channel of internal communication about security objectives and results.

controls.name: Code of Conduct
controls.summary: Maintain an approved code of conduct and obtain workforce acknowledgment at hire and periodically thereafter.
controls.statement: Maintain a code of conduct, approved by {{ conduct_approver }}, that sets expectations for integrity, ethical behavior, conflicts of interest, and protection of company and customer information, and states disciplinary consequences for violations. Require every employee and contractor to acknowledge the code within {{ acknowledgment_window }} of starting and {{ reacknowledgment_frequency }} thereafter.
controls.objective: Every workforce member has been informed of, and has agreed to, the organization's standards of conduct and the consequences of violating them.
controls.guidance: Collect acknowledgments through the HRIS or compliance platform during onboarding and annual policy attestations, and keep the signed record per person. Reference the whistleblower channel (OGRL-GV-05) in the code. Auditors typically sample new hires and existing staff for timely acknowledgment.

mappings.summary: An acknowledged code of conduct establishes standards of integrity and ethics; tone from leadership and evaluation of adherence go further.
Stated disciplinary consequences and individual acknowledgment support accountability for conduct.

controls.name: Whistleblower and Anonymous Reporting Channel
controls.summary: Provide a confidential, optionally anonymous channel for reporting ethics, fraud, and security concerns, and triage every report.
controls.statement: Provide a confidential reporting channel, with an anonymous option, through which workforce members and {{ external_reporters }} can report suspected misconduct, fraud, or security concerns. Route reports to {{ report_recipient }}, independent of the party reported on, triage each report within {{ triage_sla }}, record its disposition, and prohibit retaliation against good-faith reporters.
controls.objective: Concerns about misconduct or security can be raised safely and reach someone with authority to act, and every report is resolved.
controls.guidance: A third-party hotline or a web form that does not record identity satisfies the anonymous option; a shared inbox read only by the CEO does not provide independence if the CEO is the subject. Publish the channel in the code of conduct and employee handbook. Keep a case log (date, category, owner, outcome) as evidence; an empty log is acceptable if the channel's existence and communication are shown.

report_recipient.label: Report recipient
report_recipient.value: a designated board member or the head of legal or people operations

mappings.summary: Triaging reports of misconduct supports identifying and addressing deviations from expected conduct.
A confidential reporting channel provides a separate internal communication path for raising concerns.

controls.name: Security Objectives and Performance Measures
controls.summary: Define measurable security objectives and report performance against them to leadership on a fixed cadence.
controls.statement: Define security objectives for in-scope systems, each with at least one measurable performance metric and target, approved by {{ metrics_owner }}. Collect the metrics {{ metrics_collection_frequency }} and report results, trends, and missed targets to {{ metrics_audience }} {{ metrics_reporting_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Security objectives are specific enough to assess risk and performance against, and leadership sees measured results over time.
controls.guidance: Pick a small set of metrics tied to commitments: vulnerability SLA adherence, access review completion, training completion, MFA coverage, mean time to detect and resolve incidents, availability against SLA. Most can be pulled automatically from the compliance platform, ticketing, and monitoring. Evidence: the objectives document and dated metric reports.

mappings.summary: Developing, monitoring, and reporting security metrics meets the security half of this requirement; privacy measures are not covered.
Measurable security objectives give a clear basis for identifying and assessing risks to achieving them.
Periodic metric reporting is a form of ongoing evaluation of whether controls are performing.

controls.name: External Commitments and Customer Communication
controls.summary: Document security, availability, and confidentiality commitments made to customers, publish them, and give advance notice of material changes.
controls.statement: Maintain a register of the security, availability, and confidentiality commitments made to customers and users (for example in terms of service, data processing agreements, SLAs, and the trust center). Make current commitments and instructions for reporting security issues available through {{ customer_channel }}, notify affected customers at least {{ change_notice_period }} before a material reduction in commitments takes effect, and review the register {{ commitment_review_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Customers know what the organization has committed to and how to raise security concerns, and commitments do not change without notice.
controls.guidance: Legal or the commercial owner usually maintains the register; security confirms each commitment is backed by a control. A public trust center or security page with a security contact (for example security.txt) covers the publication channel. Evidence: the register, the published page, and notices sent for changes.

change_notice_period.label: Advance notice for material commitment changes

customer_channel.label: Customer communication channel
customer_channel.value: the public trust center and customer contracts

mappings.summary: Publishing commitments and a security contact covers communication with customers; communication with other external parties is outside this control.

controls.name: System Description and Security Plan
controls.summary: Maintain an approved description of each in-scope system covering its boundary, components, data, and controls, and keep it current.
controls.statement: Maintain a system description for each in-scope system that documents its boundary, infrastructure and software components, subservice organizations and other dependencies, data flows, information types handled, user roles, and the controls in place. The description is approved by {{ plan_approver }}, distributed to {{ plan_distribution }}, stored where only its owners can modify it, reviewed {{ plan_review_frequency }}, and updated when the system or its environment changes significantly or assessments identify problems.
controls.objective: An accurate, approved account of each system's scope and controls exists and is available to those who rely on it.
controls.guidance: This is the document a SOC 2 report's system description is drawn from. Keep the architecture and data-flow diagrams generated from or reconciled with the component inventory (OGRL-AM-01). Link controls to the OGRL control set rather than restating them. Evidence: the current version, its approval, and change history.

plan_approver.label: System description approver
plan_approver.value: the security leader and the system owner

plan_distribution.label: Recipients of the system description and changes
plan_distribution.value: engineering leadership, the compliance team, and auditors

mappings.summary: The system description covers boundary, environment, connections, and periodic updates but not approved non-applicable requirements or per-requirement implementation detail.
Covers components, operational context, roles, information types, dependencies, and controls; security categorization, privacy risk results, and design risk determinations are not required.
Distribution of the description and its changes to named recipients meets the plan distribution requirement.
Periodic review of the system description meets the plan review requirement.
Updating on significant change or assessment findings meets the plan update requirement.
Restricting modification to owners protects the plan from unauthorized change; disclosure protection relies on repository access controls.
A maintained system description is a key source of relevant, quality information about system scope and controls.
Sharing the system description with auditors and customers communicates system boundaries and controls externally.

controls.name: Acceptable Use and Rules of Behavior
controls.summary: Publish an acceptable use policy and obtain acknowledgment before access is granted and periodically thereafter.
controls.statement: Maintain an acceptable use policy that sets out workforce responsibilities and expected behavior when using company systems, devices, and data. Require each workforce member to acknowledge the policy before access to company systems is granted, and to re-acknowledge it {{ reacknowledgment_frequency }} and after material revisions. Review and update the policy {{ aup_review_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Everyone with system access has agreed to defined rules for using systems and data before receiving access, and the rules stay current.
controls.guidance: Cover device security, approved software and SaaS, handling of customer data, use of AI tools, personal use, and reporting of suspected incidents. Gate account provisioning (OGRL-AC-01) on a recorded acknowledgment in the HRIS or compliance platform. Evidence: the policy, its review history, and per-person acknowledgment timestamps compared with access grant dates.

mappings.summary: Acknowledging the acceptable use policy makes users aware of applicable security policies, one part of 3.2.1.
Published rules, acknowledgment before access, periodic review, and periodic or revision-driven re-acknowledgment together cover every part of rules of behavior.
Acknowledged rules of behavior communicate expected conduct when using systems.
The policy and acknowledgment communicate security responsibilities to every user.
The acceptable use policy is one of the policies through which expected behavior is put into practice.

controls.name: Periodic Control Assessment
controls.summary: Independently assess whether in-scope controls are designed and operating effectively on a fixed cadence, and report the results.
controls.statement: Assess the design and operating effectiveness of in-scope controls {{ assessment_frequency }} using {{ assessor }} independent of the people who operate the controls. Each assessment follows a written plan defining scope, controls, test procedures, and roles that {{ plan_approver }} approves before testing begins, produces a written report, and delivers results to {{ results_recipients }}.
controls.objective: Leadership has periodic, independent evidence of whether controls are implemented correctly and achieving their intended outcome.
controls.guidance: An external SOC 2 audit can serve as the assessment for the controls it covers; a readiness assessment or internal audit fills gaps in years without one. Retain the approved plan, workpapers or sample lists, and the final report. Findings flow to deficiency tracking (OGRL-GV-12).

assessor.label: Assessor
assessor.value: an internal audit function or a qualified third-party assessor

results_recipients.label: Recipients of assessment results
results_recipients.value: executive leadership and the board or its designated committee

mappings.summary: Planned, independent control assessments at a defined frequency meet 3.12.1 and add reporting requirements.
Covers assessor selection, an approved assessment plan, periodic assessment, reporting, and distribution of results.
Periodic independent assessment is a separate evaluation; ongoing evaluations are addressed by continuous monitoring.
Assessment results inform whether selected control activities adequately mitigate risk.

controls.name: Continuous Control Monitoring
controls.summary: Automatically test in-scope controls on an ongoing basis, act on failures, and report control health to leadership.
controls.statement: Continuously monitor in-scope controls using automated checks that track {{ monitored_metrics }}, executed {{ monitoring_frequency }}. Assign an owner and a remediation ticket to each failing check within {{ triage_sla }}, and report control health and trends to {{ status_audience }} {{ status_reporting_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Control failures between periodic assessments are detected quickly, assigned, and resolved, and leadership sees current control health.
controls.guidance: Compliance automation platforms and cloud security posture tools provide most checks out of the box (MFA enforcement, encryption at rest, logging enabled, offboarding completed, background checks on file). Tune checks to the controls in scope, route failures to the owning team's queue, and retain the dashboard history. Persistent failures become deficiencies under OGRL-GV-12.

monitored_metrics.label: Monitored control metrics
monitored_metrics.value: pass or fail status of automated control tests and open failures by age and severity

status_audience.label: Control health report audience
status_audience.value: the security leader and executive leadership

mappings.summary: Automated, ongoing monitoring of in-scope controls with triage of failures meets 3.12.3.
Defines the control metrics that automated monitoring tracks.
Automated checks provide ongoing monitoring of the defined metrics.
Owner assignment and remediation tickets for failing checks are the response actions to monitoring results.
Regular control health reporting to named recipients meets the status reporting requirement.
Automated checks are ongoing evaluations of control operation; separate evaluations are covered by periodic assessment.
Automated configuration checks detect drift that could introduce vulnerabilities.

controls.name: Deficiency Tracking and Remediation
controls.summary: Track every control deficiency to remediation with an owner and due date, and review open items with leadership.
controls.statement: Record every control deficiency identified by assessments, audits, continuous monitoring, penetration tests, or incidents in a deficiency register with an owner, severity, remediation plan, and due date. Remediate deficiencies within {{ remediation_sla }}, review open and overdue items with {{ review_audience }} {{ review_frequency }}, and escalate items past due to executive leadership.
controls.objective: Identified control weaknesses are communicated to those who can fix them and are corrected in a timely, tracked way.
controls.guidance: A dedicated project in the ticketing system or the compliance platform's findings module works as the register. Close items only with evidence of the fix and, for significant deficiencies, a retest. Evidence: the register with timestamps and the review meeting notes.

remediation_sla.label: Deficiency remediation deadline
remediation_sla.value: 30 days for high severity and 90 days for others, unless a documented risk acceptance applies

review_audience.label: Deficiency review audience
review_audience.value: the security leader and responsible control owners

mappings.summary: A deficiency register with owners, plans, and due dates, worked to closure, serves as the plan of action for 3.12.2.
The deficiency register is the plan of action and milestones, updated on a fixed cadence from assessment, audit, and monitoring findings.
Recording, reviewing, and escalating deficiencies communicates them to the parties responsible for corrective action.

controls.name: CMMC Self-Assessment, SPRS Submission, and Annual Affirmation
controls.summary: Perform the required CMMC assessment, record results in SPRS, close POA&Ms within 180 days, and affirm compliance annually.
controls.statement: Complete {{ cmmc_assessment_type }} for the documented CMMC assessment scope before award of any contract that requires it and {{ cmmc_assessment_frequency }} thereafter; ensure the results are recorded in SPRS, including the CMMC level, status date, assessment scope, the CAGE codes associated with the assessed systems, and, for Level 2, the overall score and any POA&M; close every POA&M item and complete a POA&M closeout assessment within 180 days of the Conditional CMMC status date; and have {{ affirming_official }} submit an affirmation of continuing compliance in SPRS after each assessment, after each POA&M closeout, and annually thereafter.
controls.objective: The organization holds a current CMMC status in SPRS for each assessed scope, closes any POA&M on time, and a senior official affirms continuing compliance at every required point.
controls.guidance: Under 32 CFR part 170, Level 1 self-assessments repeat annually and must be fully met with no POA&M. Level 2 self-assessments and Level 2 C3PAO certification assessments repeat every three years. A Level 2 POA&M is permitted only within the limits of 32 CFR 170.21, and the resulting Conditional status expires if closeout is not achieved within 180 days. Self-assessment results are entered in SPRS through PIEE by a user with the appropriate SPRS role; C3PAO results are uploaded by the C3PAO and appear in SPRS. The Affirming Official is the senior representative responsible for the organization's CMMC compliance and needs their own SPRS access. Before each annual affirmation, review the system security plan, recent control assessments, and open deficiencies rather than signing on trust. Keep the scope, CAGE codes, and status dates on the compliance calendar, and check contract clauses such as DFARS 252.204-7021 for any other notification obligations.

affirming_official.label: Affirming Official
affirming_official.value: the senior official designated as the Affirming Official for the organization's CMMC compliance

cmmc_assessment_frequency.label: CMMC assessment cadence
cmmc_assessment_frequency.value: annually for Level 1 self-assessments and at least every three years for Level 2 self-assessments or certification assessments

cmmc_assessment_type.label: Required CMMC level and assessment type
cmmc_assessment_type.value: the CMMC level and assessment type (Level 1 self-assessment, Level 2 self-assessment, or Level 2 C3PAO certification assessment) required by the organization's DoD contracts

controls.name: Background Screening
controls.summary: Screen employees and contractors before they receive access to production systems or customer data, and rescreen when risk changes.
controls.statement: Complete {{ screening_scope }} for every employee and contractor, to the extent permitted by applicable law, before granting access to production systems or customer data, and rescreen personnel {{ rescreening_conditions }}.
controls.objective: Reduce insider risk by confirming that individuals entrusted with systems and data have been vetted before access is granted.
controls.guidance: Use a background-check provider integrated with the HRIS or applicant tracking system so the check status gates the access-provisioning ticket. Calibrate check depth to the role and jurisdiction, document local-law exceptions, and retain completion records (not report contents) as audit evidence. Contractors supplied through an agency may be covered by the agency's screening if the contract requires it.

rescreening_conditions.label: Conditions that trigger rescreening
rescreening_conditions.value: upon transfer into a privileged or high-risk role

screening_scope.label: Required screening checks
screening_scope.value: identity verification, criminal history, and employment history checks

mappings.summary: Pre-access screening meets 3.9.1 when the screened access includes all systems containing CUI, not only production or customer data.
Screening before access plus condition-based rescreening covers both parts of PS-3.
Vetting personnel supports the integrity expectations of CC1.1 but does not address the broader tone and conduct standards.
Pre-access screening is one element of the workforce competence and trustworthiness expectations in CC1.4.

controls.name: Personnel Offboarding
controls.summary: Run a documented offboarding checklist for every departure and an access review for every internal transfer.
controls.statement: For every departing employee or contractor, complete a documented offboarding checklist that disables system access within {{ access_disable_sla }} of separation, revokes associated credentials, keys, and tokens, recovers company-issued devices and sanitizes them before reassignment, briefs the individual on {{ exit_briefing_topics }}, and transfers ownership of the individual's data and systems to a designated owner; when an individual transfers roles, review and adjust existing access to match the new role within {{ transfer_review_sla }}.
controls.objective: Ensure departing and transferring personnel retain no access, credentials, or company assets beyond what their current status requires.
controls.guidance: Trigger the checklist automatically from the HRIS termination or job-change event into the ticketing system. Use the identity provider to suspend SSO and revoke sessions, then sweep systems outside SSO (cloud root or break-glass credentials, SSH keys, personal access tokens, API keys). Track device return through the MDM inventory and remote-wipe unreturned devices. Account disablement itself is also governed by OGRL-AC-01; this control evidences the full offboarding workflow.

access_disable_sla.label: Maximum time to disable access after separation

exit_briefing_topics.label: Topics covered in the exit briefing
exit_briefing_topics.value: continuing confidentiality obligations and return of company property

transfer_review_sla.label: Time to review access after an internal transfer

mappings.summary: Documented offboarding with timely access revocation and role- change access review protects systems through terminations and transfers.
The offboarding checklist covers access disablement, credential revocation, exit briefing, property recovery, and retained data access required by PS-4.
The transfer access review confirms continued need for existing access when personnel change roles.
Adjusting access to match the new role after a transfer is the modification PS-5(c) calls for.
Removing credentials and access at separation and transfer contributes to CC6.2; account registration and authorization are covered elsewhere.
Recovering and sanitizing devices from departing personnel contributes to CC6.5 but does not cover general asset disposal.

controls.name: Confidentiality and Access Agreements
controls.summary: Require signed confidentiality and acceptable-use agreements before access, and refresh acknowledgements periodically.
controls.statement: Require every employee and contractor to sign a confidentiality agreement and acknowledge the acceptable use and information security policies before receiving access to systems or confidential information; review the agreement templates {{ agreement_review_frequency }} and obtain renewed acknowledgement {{ reacknowledgement_frequency }} and whenever the agreements materially change.
controls.objective: Establish enforceable, documented obligations for protecting organizational and customer information before anyone is given access to it.
controls.guidance: Collect signatures through the HRIS or e-signature tool during onboarding and gate access provisioning on completion. Track annual re-acknowledgement alongside awareness training to reduce friction. Legal should own the templates; security should own the policy content they reference.

mappings.summary: Documented agreements signed before access, periodically reviewed, and re-signed on change or cadence satisfy PS-6.
Binding personnel to confidentiality obligations contributes to protecting confidential information under C1.1.
Signed policy acknowledgements help communicate and enforce expected conduct, one aspect of CC1.1.

controls.name: Contractor and Third-Party Personnel Security
controls.summary: Hold external personnel with system access to the organization's personnel security requirements and require timely notice of their departures.
controls.statement: Require providers whose personnel access organizational systems or confidential data to apply the organization's personnel security requirements, including screening, confidentiality agreements, and security training, with roles and responsibilities documented in the contract; require the provider to notify {{ notification_recipient }} of any transfer or termination of such personnel within {{ notification_window }}; and verify provider compliance {{ compliance_verification_frequency }}.
controls.objective: Ensure external personnel with access meet the same security expectations as employees and lose access promptly when their engagement ends.
controls.guidance: Sponsor every contractor account through an internal owner and give it an end date in the identity provider. Include personnel security clauses in staffing agreements and request attestation of screening and training completion. Reconcile active contractor accounts against the provider's roster as part of verification.

notification_recipient.label: Recipient of provider personnel change notices
notification_recipient.value: the internal sponsor and the security team

mappings.summary: Contractual personnel security requirements, change notifications, and compliance verification cover each part of PS-7.
Extending screening and training expectations to external personnel supports the workforce expectations of CC1.4.
Imposing personnel security obligations on providers addresses one dimension of vendor risk management under CC9.2.

controls.name: Personnel Sanctions
controls.summary: Apply a documented disciplinary process to security and privacy policy violations and notify designated roles when it is invoked.
controls.statement: Apply the documented disciplinary process to any employee or contractor who violates information security or privacy policies, record each case and its outcome, and notify {{ sanction_notification_recipient }} within {{ sanction_notification_window }} when a formal sanction is initiated, identifying the individual and the reason.
controls.objective: Hold personnel accountable for policy violations consistently and ensure security leadership is aware of sanctioned individuals.
controls.guidance: Reference the sanctions process in the code of conduct and acceptable use policy. HR owns case records; security receives notification so it can review the individual's access. Keep a log of cases (even if empty for the period) to evidence operation.

sanction_notification_recipient.label: Roles notified when a sanction is initiated
sanction_notification_recipient.value: the security lead and the individual's manager

mappings.summary: A formal sanctions process with timely notification of designated roles satisfies both parts of PS-8.
Consistently addressing deviations from expected conduct supports the integrity commitments of CC1.1.
Disciplinary action for security violations is a mechanism for holding individuals accountable under CC1.5.

controls.name: Position Descriptions and Security Responsibilities
controls.summary: Document security and privacy responsibilities in every job description and keep them current.
controls.statement: Include security and privacy responsibilities in the documented description of every position, with role-specific duties for {{ elevated_roles }}, and review position descriptions {{ description_review_frequency }} and when roles materially change.
controls.objective: Make each individual's security and privacy obligations explicit so they can be communicated, trained, and enforced.
controls.guidance: Add a standard security-responsibilities clause to all job descriptions and role-specific clauses for engineering, operations, and leadership roles. Store current descriptions in the HRIS or a controlled document repository and record review dates.

elevated_roles.label: Roles requiring role-specific security duties
elevated_roles.value: engineers, administrators, and security and privacy personnel

mappings.summary: The control incorporates security and privacy responsibilities into position descriptions as PS-9 requires and adds periodic review.
Defining security responsibilities per position supports the assignment of responsibilities addressed by CC1.3.
Documented role expectations provide a basis for hiring and developing competent personnel under CC1.4.

controls.name: Security and Privacy Awareness Training
controls.summary: Train all personnel in security and privacy awareness at onboarding and on a recurring cadence, reinforced by phishing simulations.
controls.statement: Require every employee and contractor to complete security and privacy awareness training within {{ onboarding_training_window }} of starting and {{ training_frequency }} thereafter; conduct simulated phishing exercises {{ phishing_simulation_frequency }}; and update training content {{ content_review_frequency }} and after {{ content_update_events }}, incorporating lessons learned from security incidents.
controls.objective: Equip all personnel to recognize and report threats and to handle information in line with security and privacy policies.
controls.guidance: Use a training platform integrated with the HRIS so new hires are enrolled automatically and completion is tracked; escalate overdue training to managers and consider suspending access after a grace period. Cover phishing, credential hygiene, data handling, incident reporting, and privacy basics. Feed internal incidents and phishing simulation results into content updates.

content_update_events.label: Events that trigger content updates
content_update_events.value: significant security incidents, policy changes, or emerging threats

onboarding_training_window.label: Deadline for initial training after start date

mappings.summary: Recurring awareness training makes users aware of security risks but does not itself cover identifying CUI risks or applicable procedures.
Simulated phishing exercises are practical exercises that simulate real attack events.
Training at onboarding and on a recurring cadence covers initial and periodic literacy training.
Simulated phishing exercises are the awareness technique the control employs.
Content is updated on a defined cadence and after defined events.
Lessons learned from security incidents are incorporated into training content.
Recurring security training develops personnel competence, one element of CC1.4.
Awareness training is a primary channel for communicating security responsibilities internally under CC2.2.

controls.name: Role-Based Security Training
controls.summary: Provide additional security training tailored to roles with elevated access or security-relevant duties.
controls.statement: Provide role-specific security training to {{ trained_roles }} before they are granted access to perform those duties, {{ role_training_frequency }} thereafter, and when significant system changes alter their responsibilities; update the content {{ role_content_review_frequency }} and after {{ role_content_update_events }}, incorporating lessons learned from security incidents.
controls.objective: Ensure personnel with elevated access or security duties have the specific knowledge needed to perform them securely.
controls.guidance: Typical modules include secure coding and OWASP topics for engineers, cloud and IAM hygiene for infrastructure administrators, incident handling for on-call responders, and privacy obligations for staff handling personal data. Track completion per role in the training platform and gate production access requests on completion.

role_content_update_events.label: Events that trigger role-based content updates
role_content_update_events.value: significant security incidents or major technology changes

trained_roles.label: Roles requiring role-based training
trained_roles.value: engineers with production or source code access, on-call incident responders, and administrators of in-scope systems

mappings.summary: Role-based training covers training personnel for security duties but not defining and assigning those duties.
Role-specific training before access, on a cadence, on system change, with content updates and lessons learned covers all parts of AT-3.
Role-specific training develops the competence of personnel in security-relevant roles, part of CC1.4.
Role-based training communicates role-specific security responsibilities, one aspect of CC2.2.

controls.name: Insider Threat Awareness Training
controls.summary: Train managers and employees to recognize and report potential indicators of insider threat.
controls.statement: Document the potential indicators of insider threat relevant to the organization, including {{ insider_threat_indicators }}; train every manager, employee, and contractor to recognize these indicators and to report them through {{ insider_threat_reporting_channel }} within {{ insider_threat_training_window }} of starting and {{ insider_threat_training_frequency }} thereafter; and keep records of training completion.
controls.objective: Managers and employees can recognize potential indicators of insider threat and know how to report them.
controls.guidance: Deliver this as a module in the annual security awareness course (OGRL-HR-07) and track completion on the same platform. Give managers extra material on spotting behavioral changes and on escalating concerns to HR and security without investigating on their own. Keep the reporting channel simple and offer a confidential or anonymous option. Work with HR and legal so the indicators focus on behavior, not protected characteristics. Cleared contractors subject to 32 CFR part 117 have separate, more extensive insider threat program requirements.

insider_threat_indicators.label: Documented potential indicators of insider threat
insider_threat_indicators.value: long-term job dissatisfaction, attempts to access information not required for job duties, unexplained access to financial resources, bullying or harassment of coworkers, workplace violence, and other serious violations of organizational policies

insider_threat_reporting_channel.label: Channel for reporting potential insider threat indicators
insider_threat_reporting_channel.value: the security team's reporting address or a confidential ethics hotline

insider_threat_training_window.label: Deadline for initial insider threat training after start

mappings.summary: Documented insider threat indicators and recurring training for managers and employees meet 3.2.3.
Training staff to recognize and report insider threat indicators meets AT-2(2).

controls.name: Incident Response Plan and Tabletop Testing
controls.summary: Maintain a documented security incident response plan and exercise it regularly through tabletop or simulated drills.
controls.statement: Maintain a documented security incident response plan with defined roles and escalation paths, and test response effectiveness {{ ir_test_cadence }} using {{ ir_test_method }}.
controls.objective: Ensure personnel can rapidly detect, contain, eradicate, recover from, and report security incidents.
controls.guidance: Document post-incident lessons learned, track corrective action items to closure, and update contact trees whenever on-call rotations or regulatory notification obligations change.

ir_test_method.label: Incident response test method
ir_test_method.value: structured tabletop exercises and simulated incident drills

tests.name: Verify Annual Incident Response Tabletop Exercise
tests.description: Examine the current incident response plan, after-action report from the most recent tabletop exercise, and closure evidence for identified follow-up tasks.

mappings.summary: A documented response plan with roles and escalation provides the preparation element of the incident-handling capability; it also covers testing.
Testing the incident response plan on a defined cadence fully meets 3.6.3, and the control also requires the plan itself.
Periodic incident response tabletop drills satisfy SP 800-171 03.06.03.
Scheduled tabletop exercises and drills directly satisfy NIST IR-3 incident response testing.
Incident response playbooks and exercises support event evaluation and response under SOC 2 CC7.3.
A documented, tested response plan defines how identified incidents are responded to under CC7.4.

controls.name: Incident Handling and Triage
controls.summary: Triage suspected security incidents promptly against a defined severity scale and drive confirmed incidents through containment, eradication, and recovery.
controls.statement: Triage each suspected security incident within {{ triage_sla }} of it being reported or detected, classify it using {{ severity_scale }}, assign an incident commander, and handle confirmed incidents through containment, eradication, and recovery as defined in the incident response plan, escalating high-severity incidents to {{ escalation_contacts }}.
controls.objective: Ensure suspected incidents are evaluated quickly and consistently and that confirmed incidents are contained and resolved before they cause further harm.
controls.guidance: Route monitoring alerts and employee or customer reports into a single on-call intake such as a paging tool or dedicated incident channel. Define a severity matrix (for example SEV1-SEV4) keyed on data exposure, customer impact, and blast radius. Keep runbooks for common cloud SaaS scenarios such as compromised credentials, leaked secrets, malicious dependencies, and cloud account takeover: revoke sessions and keys, isolate workloads with security groups or by scaling to zero, and snapshot volumes and preserve logs for forensics before rebuilding. Coordinate with the disaster recovery plan when recovery requires restoration from backup. Evidence is the incident ticket showing triage time, severity, commander, and response actions.

escalation_contacts.label: High-severity escalation contacts
escalation_contacts.value: the security lead and executive leadership

mappings.summary: Triage, analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery of detected or reported incidents make up most of the operational capability; preparation and user response activities are not covered.
Severity-based triage and plan-driven containment, eradication, and recovery implement the incident handling capability in IR-4(a).
A shared severity matrix and runbooks make incident handling consistent, contributing to the predictability IR-4(d) expects across the organization.
Triage and severity classification determine whether security events are incidents requiring response.
Containment, eradication, and recovery steps form the core of the organization's incident response activity.

controls.name: Incident Tracking and Documentation
controls.summary: Record every security incident in a tracking system from detection through closure with a consistent set of required details.
controls.statement: Record every security incident in {{ incident_tracking_system }} from detection through closure, capturing at minimum the detection source, timeline, severity, affected systems and data, actions taken, responsible owner, and resolution, and retain incident records for {{ incident_record_retention }}.
controls.objective: Maintain a complete and reliable history of incidents that supports coordinated response, trend analysis, and audit evidence.
controls.guidance: Use a dedicated ticket type or project with mandatory fields rather than free-form chat threads, and link alerts, incident channel exports, and post-incident reviews to the record. Restrict who can delete incident records. Report incident counts, time to detect, and time to resolve to leadership periodically. Auditors typically sample incidents for completeness, so keep the register even in periods with no incidents and document that none occurred.

incident_tracking_system.label: Incident tracking system
incident_tracking_system.value: a dedicated incident ticket queue with mandatory fields

mappings.summary: Tracking and documenting every incident from detection through closure meets the tracking and documentation objectives of 3.6.2.
Recording every incident with required details through closure satisfies IR-5 incident tracking and documentation.
Documented incident records evidence how security events were evaluated and classified.
Incident records capture the response actions taken, supporting a defined and evidenced response process.

controls.name: Incident Reporting and Customer Notification
controls.summary: Require prompt internal reporting of suspected incidents and notify affected customers and authorities of confirmed incidents within defined deadlines.
controls.statement: Require personnel to report suspected security incidents to the security team through a published reporting channel within {{ internal_report_window }} of discovery, and report confirmed incidents affecting customer data or services to {{ external_notification_recipients }} within {{ external_notification_deadline }} of confirmation, or sooner where contract or law requires.
controls.objective: Ensure incidents reach the response team quickly and that external parties who rely on the system learn of incidents affecting them in time to protect themselves.
controls.guidance: Publish a reporting channel such as a security@ alias or chat channel and cover it in onboarding and awareness training. Maintain a notification matrix of contractual (MSA, DPA) and regulatory deadlines, such as GDPR supervisory-authority notice within 72 hours or public-company disclosure rules, and have legal review external notices. Keep pre-approved notification templates and use the status page for availability incidents. Retain copies of sent notifications as evidence.

external_notification_recipients.label: External incident notification recipients
external_notification_recipients.value: affected customers, regulators, law enforcement, and other parties as required by contract or law

mappings.summary: Identifies internal and external report recipients and requires them to be notified, covering the reporting objectives of 3.6.2.
Mandatory internal reporting of suspected incidents within a set window satisfies IR-6(a).
